docs.title: Introduction to GIS
docs.text: Welcome to a 12-week, project-based journey through Geographic Information Systems. This course begins with hands-on QGIS skills and gradually transitions into Python-based analysis, helping you move from point-and-click workflows to reproducible code.

docs.title: Course structure
docs.text:
Weeks Focus Tools 1-6 GIS foundations QGIS 7 Bridge to Python Anaconda, Jupyter 8-10 Python automation GeoPandas, Rasterio, OSMnx 11-12 Design & capstone QGIS + Python

Capstone project: You'll work on a spatial project throughout all 12 weeks, not just at the end. Start thinking about your topic in Week 1.

docs.title: Step 1: Set up your tools
docs.text:
1. Install QGIS
  2. Set up your workspace
  3. Download Week 1 data

docs.title: Step 2: Do the readings
docs.text:
Before Week 1, read:

  • What is GIS? (15 min)
  • Your Capstone Project (10 min)

docs.title: Step 3: Start Week 1
docs.text: Head to Week 1 Lab and begin your GIS journey.

docs.title: Who this course is for
docs.text:
• Students new to spatial analysis and mapping
  • Researchers working with geographic data
  • Professionals needing GIS skills for planning, health, environment, or policy work
  • Self-learners building a portfolio in geospatial analysis

Prerequisites: No prior GIS or programming experience required. Basic computer skills assumed (file management, installing software).

docs.title: Your responsibilities
docs.text: This course requires initiative and preparation. Success depends on you taking ownership of your learning.

docs.title: Before each class
docs.text:
• Complete the readings and download the required data
  • Set up your folder structure and verify your software works
  • If you have issues, contact the teaching team BEFORE class — we cannot troubleshoot installations or missing data during lab time

docs.title: For your capstone project
docs.text:
• Discuss your project idea with the teaching team early — don't wait until Week 10
  • Come with a topic area and initial questions; we'll help you refine them
  • Try to find data sources yourself first, then ask for guidance if stuck
  • Check in at milestones (Weeks 3, 5, 7, 10) to stay on track

docs.title: Asking for help
docs.text:
We're here to support you, but we expect you to:

  1. Try first — attempt the problem, read error messages, check the documentation
  2. Be specific — "It doesn't work" isn't helpful; "I get this error when I try to join these tables" is
  3. Come prepared — have your data ready, your project open, and your question clear

The teaching team wants you to succeed

We're happy to help with guidance, troubleshooting, and feedback — but the learning happens when you do the work. Take initiative, ask questions, and engage with the material.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course you will be able to:

  1. Use QGIS confidently for mapping and spatial analysis
  2. Understand coordinate systems, projections, and data formats
  3. Join data to boundaries and create thematic maps
  4. Perform hotspot analysis, accessibility modelling, and terrain analysis
  5. Automate workflows with Python and GeoPandas
  6. Design accessible, publication-ready maps
  7. Complete a portfolio-ready capstone project

docs.text: These pages capture instructor-facing lecture notes, brainstorming lists, and other planning material. They are grouped under Course Development in the navigation and are not intended for learners. When the course is published, you can hide or remove this section if desired.

docs.title: Week 1 Lecture · Foundations of GIS
docs.text: Set the tone for the course by introducing what GIS is, how it is used, and the mind-set shift from spreadsheets to spatial storytelling.

docs.title: Lecture objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session learners should be able to:

  1. Articulate a working definition of GIS and describe why “where” matters in data analysis.
  2. Distinguish between vector and raster data models and cite everyday examples of each.
  3. Recognise the importance of metadata (coordinate reference systems, extent, resolution, vintage) when evaluating spatial datasets.
  4. Connect the lecture material to the Week 1 lab, which focuses on exploring the QGIS interface and inspecting Natural Earth datasets.

docs.title: 1. Why GIS? (Slides 1–4)
docs.text:
• Define GIS as the integration of spatial and attribute data, supported by hardware, software, and people.
  • Use scenarios from transport planning, emergency response, and public health to show real-world impact.
  • Reference the Esri overview article and pull 2–3 quotable stats or graphics.

docs.title: 2. Spatial vs tabular thinking (Slides 5–7)
docs.text:
• Contrast a traditional spreadsheet of addresses with a geocoded point map to emphasise pattern recognition.
  • Introduce the idea of “scale” (global → regional → local) and how questions change at each level.
  • Highlight the concept of geographic context (proximity, adjacency, containment).

docs.title: 3. Data models: Vector & raster (Slides 8–11)
docs.text:
• Vector: point (bus stop), line (river, road), polygon (suburb, LGA). Mention topology and attribute tables.
  • Raster: grid of pixels capturing continuous phenomena (elevation, temperature, imagery). Touch on resolution and band combinations.
  • Tie back to the reading on Spatial Data Models as optional pre-reading for Week 2.

docs.title: 4. Metadata essentials (Slides 12–14)
docs.text:
• Break down CRS (geographic vs projected), why mismatched CRS produce misaligned layers, and examples relevant to Australia (EPSG:7856) and global datasets (EPSG:4326).
  • Cover extent, resolution, vintage, and licensing. Provide a screenshot of the QGIS layer properties panel showing metadata fields.

docs.title: 5. GIS workflow building blocks (Slides 15–17)
docs.text:
• Introduce the lightweight GIS workflow learners will practise: acquire data → inspect metadata → clean/format → analyse/visualise → communicate.
  • Position QGIS as the “hands-on” environment they will use in Weeks 1–6 before transitioning to automation.
  • Include a slide referencing the Week 1 lab outcomes (set up project, load Natural Earth, export a quick map).

docs.title: 6. Closing & reflection (Slides 18–19)
docs.text:
• Summarise key takeaways and preview the next lecture (cartographic conventions).
  • Prompt learners to jot down one domain-specific question they hope to answer with GIS.

docs.title: Key vocabulary to cover
docs.text:
• GIS: Geographic Information System (integration of spatial + attribute data for analysis/visualisation).
  • Spatial data: Data that includes location (coordinates, addresses, regions).
  • Vector data: Points, lines, polygons stored with attributes.
  • Raster data: Gridded pixels storing values; often continuous phenomena.
  • Attribute table: Tabular data linked to spatial features.
  • Coordinate Reference System (CRS): Framework used to map the Earth’s surface (e.g., WGS84, GDA2020).
  • Metadata: “Data about data” — provides context such as source, scale, resolution, date, license.

docs.title: Live demo ideas
docs.text:
• Demonstrate a CSV-to-map moment: show a table of city names/coordinates, then drag into QGIS to plot points.
  • Open the Natural Earth Admin 0 shapefile and inspect the attribute table; highlight how fields connect to the map.
  • Display layer properties to point out CRS, extent, and licensing information.
  • Use the Identify tool on a feature to reinforce the link between map and attribute data.

docs.title: Sample case-study snippets
docs.text:
• Transport: Mapping train station catchments to illustrate first/last mile challenges.
  • Health: Visualising vaccination clinic locations versus population density to reveal gaps.
  • Environment: Overlaying flood-prone areas with housing to discuss resilience planning.

docs.title: On-slide callouts & visuals
docs.text:
• Diagram showing layers stacking (basemap, points, polygons) akin to a “data sandwich.”
  • Graphic comparing vector and raster data side-by-side (e.g., polygon boundary vs DEM tile).
  • Screenshot of QGIS interface labelled with Browser, Layers, Processing Toolbox panels.
  • Map highlighting CRS mismatch (misaligned layers) versus corrected alignment.

docs.title: Discussion prompts
docs.text:
• Where have you encountered GIS outputs in everyday life (navigation apps, weather, election maps)?
  • What decisions in your field could change if you understood spatial context better?
  • What concerns or opportunities do you see when combining location data with people-centric datasets?

docs.title: Instructor tips
docs.text:
• Gauge prior experience with a quick show-of-hands or poll (GIS novices vs experienced users).
  • Use local datasets/examples to make the content tangible for your cohort.
  • Keep the lecture interactive—pose questions after each section and invite learners to share domain-specific examples.
  • Reinforce that the upcoming lab is exploratory; perfection is not expected.

docs.title: Suggested follow-up for learners
docs.text:
• Complete the readings and jot down one question to raise during lab.
  • Make sure QGIS opens without errors and you can locate the intro-to-gis-course workspace.
  • Download the Natural Earth layers ahead of the lab (see Downloading datasets).

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
1. Understand the essential elements every map should include (title, legend, scale, north arrow when needed, data credits).
  2. Apply cartographic conventions to colour, typography, and symbol hierarchy.
  3. Recognise colour connotations and accessibility considerations when styling thematic maps.

docs.title: Lecture outline
docs.text:
1. Purpose-driven mapping
  2. Audience and message first.
  3. Relationship between map type (choropleth, proportional symbol, dot density) and data structure.
  4. Map essentials checklist
  5. Title/subtitle, legend, scale bar, north arrow (conditional), data/method credits, source links.
  6. Demonstrate how each element supports trust and interpretation.
  7. Colour theory & accessibility
  8. Sequential vs diverging vs qualitative palettes.
  9. Introduce the Esri colour connotations article.
  10. Discuss cultural interpretations (e.g., red ≠ universal danger), colour-blind safe palettes, and contrast ratios.
  11. Typography & layout
  12. Font pairing, hierarchy, alignment to grids.
  13. White space management borrowed from magazine/layout design.
  14. Link to the Layout template guide.
  15. Case studies
  16. Show good/bad map examples (e.g., misused colours, cluttered legends).
  17. Invite learners to critique using a rubric.

docs.title: Recommended readings & inspiration
docs.text:
• Esri: Colour Connotations and Associations
  • Axis Maps: Cartography Guide
  • Map Design Basics

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Connotation vs perception: how red/green/blue are interpreted differently across cultures.
  • Importance of data classification choices (equal interval, quantile, natural breaks) and how they affect perception.
  • Use of annotation and callouts drawn from graphic design (magazine spreads) to lead the reader’s eye.
  • Why every map should have explicit data and methodology attribution.

docs.title: Classroom activities
docs.text:
• Bring in magazine spreads or infographic examples and identify layout parallels.
  • Colour audit exercise: evaluate palette choices with colour-blind simulators.
  • Legend critique: swap legends and see if classmates can interpret the map without explanation.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
• Apply these conventions in the Week 2 lab when styling renewable energy choropleths and world city labels.
  • Update the exported layout checklist based on peer feedback.

docs.title: Week 3 Lecture · Boundary Systems & Data Joins
Objectives
docs.text:
• Explain why countries maintain multiple boundary hierarchies (administrative vs statistical).
  • Illustrate how boundary changes affect longitudinal analysis.
  • Review best practices for joining tabular data (SEIFA, ACS) to polygons.

docs.title: Core topics
docs.text:
1. Boundary ecosystem overview
  2. Administrative vs statistical boundaries (refer back to Understanding administrative boundaries).
  3. Who maintains them (ABS, Census, Eurostat, local councils) and release cadences.
  4. Boundary change implications
  5. Visual timeline of ASGS releases; demonstrate how SA2 splits/merges break comparisons.
  6. Strategies: rebasing, area-weighted interpolation, using correspondence files.
  7. Join fundamentals
  8. Unique keys, data types, handling nulls.
  9. Demonstrate mismatch scenarios (leading zeros, whitespace, outdated codes).
  10. Using crosswalk tables/correspondence files.
  11. Communication
  12. Documenting boundary level in maps/reports.
  13. Caution against mixing incomparable geographies (postcodes vs LGAs).

docs.title: Suggested visuals
docs.text:
• Diagram of ADM0 → ADM1 → ADM2 → statistical areas.
  • Map showing boundary revisions between ASGS 2016 vs 2021.
  • Flowchart for join process with checks (validate CRS, inspect attribute table, run spot checks).

docs.title: Activity ideas
docs.text:
• Quick boundary quiz: identify which boundary fits each policy question.
  • Join debugging: provide messy CSV with different ID formatting, have learners fix and document the process.

docs.title: Reading references
docs.text:
• Administrative boundary explainer.
  • ABS: ASGS overview.
  • ABS: Correspondence files (show where to find them).

docs.title: Link to lab
docs.text:
• Prepares learners for the Week 3 vector join exercise.
  • Reinforces why we store cleaned joins in data/processed/week03/.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Introduce digital elevation models (DEMs), hillshade, slope, and contour derivations.
  • Compare data sources (ELVIS, SRTM, LiDAR) and discuss resolution implications.
  • Explain how elevation intersects with planning contexts (flood, transport, habitat).

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. DEM fundamentals
  2. Raster structure, resolution, vertical accuracy, common file formats.
  3. Differences between DEM, DSM, DTM.
  4. Data sources
  5. Australia: ELVIS, state-based LiDAR portals.
  6. Global: SRTM, NASADEM, ASTER GDEM.
  7. Licensing and access considerations.
  8. Derived products
  9. Hillshade, slope, aspect, contour, TPI.
  10. When to use each and styling considerations.
  11. Integrating with boundaries
  12. Zonal statistics for risk assessment (e.g., elevation vs SEIFA).
  13. Communicating uncertainty (resolution, interpolation artefacts).

docs.title: Visual aids
docs.text:
• DEM vs hillshade comparison.
  • Resolution comparison (30 m vs 1 m).
  • Flowchart of raster processing pipeline (raw DEM → clip → hillshade/slope → overlay).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Geoscience Australia: ELVIS documentation.
  • USGS: SRTM Overview.
  • Raster analysis chapters from QGIS training manual.

docs.title: Connection to lab
docs.text:
• Sets context for clipping DEMs, producing hillshade, and overlaying with SA2/LGA boundaries.
  • Prepares learners for Week 5 by thinking about terrain in situational analysis.

docs.title: Week 5 Lecture · Ethics of Crime Mapping
Objectives
docs.text:
• Discuss ethical considerations when visualising crime data.
  • Highlight the impact of boundary choice, temporal aggregation, and context on public perception.
  • Provide frameworks for responsible storytelling (language, disclaimers, community engagement).

docs.title: Key discussion points
docs.text:
1. Data provenance & bias
  2. Crime data reflects reporting practices, policing priorities, and socio-economic factors.
  3. Missing context (e.g., victimisation surveys) and potential for reinforcing stereotypes.
  4. Privacy & aggregation
  5. Why many datasets aggregate to LGA, precinct, or anonymised coordinates.
  6. Balancing detail with privacy; use of jittering or hex bins.
  7. Narrative framing
  8. Use neutral language; avoid “crime hotspots” without describing contributing factors.
  9. Include socio-economic context and community assets (lighting, youth programs).
  10. Community impact
  11. Maps influence policy, property values, and stigma.
  12. Encourage learner empathy and stakeholder interviews where possible.

docs.title: Suggested readings
docs.text:
• Jerry Ratcliffe, Crime Mapping and Spatial Analysis (ethics chapter).
  • Articles on policing bias / open data guidelines (e.g., U.S. DOJ Analytic Toolkit).
  • Any local government data sharing policies.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
• Case study review: examine two crime maps with differing framing; debate potential impacts.
  • Scenario planning: how would you brief a community meeting before presenting a map?

docs.title: Link to lab
docs.text:
• Reinforces careful filtering, boundary selection, and annotation choices in Week 5’s hotspot exercise.
  • Encourage learners to document assumptions and limitations in their outputs.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Explore how spatial access to health services influences equity outcomes.
  • Introduce common accessibility metrics (catchments, drive-time, two-step floating catchment area).
  • Discuss limitations of open health datasets and ways to contextualise them.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. Health equity framing
  2. Social determinants of health; why location matters.
  3. Examples from Australian context (rural vs metropolitan service availability).
  4. Accessibility metrics
  5. Simple buffers, drive-time/isochrones, gravity models.
  6. Pros/cons of each, data requirements, and assumptions.
  7. Data considerations
  8. Facility types (primary care vs hospitals), service capacity, hours of operation.
  9. Using vulnerability indices (SEIFA, SVI) as weighting factors.
  10. Communication
  11. Appropriate language; avoid blaming communities.
  12. Present findings with action-oriented recommendations.

docs.title: Readings & resources
docs.text:
• WHO: Handbook on Health Inequality Monitoring.
  • Highlight chapters on geographic accessibility.
  • Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reports on service distribution.
  • Example research using 2SFCA or network analysis for health planning.

docs.title: Classroom activities
docs.text:
• Compare two accessibility maps (buffer vs drive-time) and discuss differences.
  • Brainstorm policy interventions based on observed gaps.

docs.title: Link to lab
docs.text: • Prepares learners for service area generation, overlay with vulnerability indices, and equity-focused storytelling in Week 6.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Map QGIS vector workflows to Python libraries (GeoPandas, Shapely, PyProj).
  • Discuss data cleaning strategies (naming conventions, handling missing values).
  • Highlight performance considerations and tooling for reproducible vector pipelines.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. From GUI to code
  2. Recap Week 3 joins and Week 5 analysis to show equivalent code snippets.
  3. Anatomy of a GeoPandas workflow (read → clean → spatial join → summarise → export).
  4. Data cleaning patterns
  5. Column normalisation, dtype conversions, dealing with multi-part geometries.
  6. Using assign, query, groupby.
  7. Spatial joins & overlays
  8. sjoin, overlay, dissolve and when to use each.
  9. Notes on projections and performance.
  10. Saving outputs
  11. GeoPackage vs GeoJSON vs Parquet; storing metadata in filenames or README.
  12. Round-tripping data back into QGIS.

docs.title: Sample code to showcase
docs.text:
neighbourhoods = gpd.read_file("data/processed/week08/neighbourhoods.geojson").to_crs(3857)
incidents = gpd.read_file("data/processed/week08/incidents.geojson").to_crs(3857)
joined = gpd.sjoin(incidents, neighbourhoods, predicate="within")
summary = (
    joined.groupby("neighbourhood_id")
    .size()
    .rename("incident_count")
    .to_frame()
    .join(neighbourhoods.set_index("neighbourhood_id"), how="right")
)
summary["rate_km2"] = summary["incident_count"] / (summary.geometry.area / 1e6)
summary.to_file("data/processed/week08/neighbourhoods_summary.gpkg", layer="summary")

docs.title: Discussion prompts
docs.text:
• What QA checks should you run after automating joins?
  • How do you balance code readability vs efficiency?
  • When would you still use QGIS manually instead of automation?

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:

  • OSMnx for graph-based spatial operations: https://osmnx.readthedocs.io/
  • Pysal for spatial statistics: https://pysal.org/

docs.title: Week 9 Lecture · Remote Sensing & Change Detection
Objectives
docs.text:
• Introduce remote sensing fundamentals (spectral bands, temporal revisits, resolutions).
  • Discuss common indices (NDVI, NDBI, NDWI) and when to use them.
  • Explain workflows for change detection between pre- and post-event imagery.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. Remote sensing basics
  2. Platforms (Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, Planet).
  3. Spatial, temporal, spectral resolution trade-offs.
  4. Preprocessing considerations (cloud masking, atmospheric correction).
  5. Vegetation & built environment indices
  6. NDVI formula: (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red); interpret scale.
  7. NDWI, NDBI, and other indices relevant to urban/environmental analysis.
  8. Change detection techniques
  9. Simple differencing (NDVI_before - NDVI_after).
  10. Thresholding and classification.
  11. Limitations (seasonality, sensor differences).
  12. Zonal statistics & reporting
  13. Summarise change by administrative boundaries (ties back to Week 3).
  14. Communicate uncertainty and limitations.

docs.title: Recommended readings
docs.text:
• ESA Sentinel-2 User Guide.
  • USGS remote sensing tutorials.
  • Articles on change detection best practices (e.g., NASA Earthdata).

docs.title: Classroom activities
docs.text:
• Compare two images (pre/post event) and identify potential false positives.
  • Debate whether change should be presented in raw index difference, percentage, or classification.

docs.title: Link to lab
docs.text: • Prepares learners for the Week 9 notebook steps: clipping rasters, computing change arrays, and summarising by zones.

docs.title: Week 10 Lecture · Network Theory for Mobility
Objectives
docs.text:
• Explain fundamental graph concepts used in transport analysis (nodes, edges, weights).
  • Introduce accessibility metrics (isochrones, betweenness, coverage, catchment ratios).
  • Discuss data sources (OpenStreetMap, GTFS) and preprocessing considerations.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. Graph fundamentals
  2. Directed vs undirected graphs, weighted edges (distance, time).
  3. Simplification levels (primal vs dual graphs) and implications for analysis.
  4. Accessibility measures
  5. Isochrones (reach in X minutes) and coverage metrics (population within catchment).
  6. Betweenness/closeness centrality for identifying critical links.
  7. Two-step floating catchment for transit/health service overlap.
  8. Data integration
  9. Working with OpenStreetMap (coverage, tagging quirks).
  10. GTFS feed components (stops, trips, stop_times) and conversion to networks.
  11. Handling coordinate reference systems and projections for network calculations.
  12. Equity & policy context
  13. Using demographic overlays to interpret accessibility, aligning with Week 6 themes.
  14. Presenting limitations (schedule granularity, assumed speeds).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
• Visualise a simple network diagram and compute sample metrics manually.
  • Review case studies (e.g., Melbourne tram accessibility, Sydney bus coverage).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• OSMnx documentation: https://osmnx.readthedocs.io/
  • Transitland / GTFS resources.
  • Academic references on accessibility modelling.

docs.title: Lab connection
docs.text: • Supports Week 10 notebook tasks (downloading network graphs, computing isochrones, intersecting with population polygons).

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Reinforce storytelling principles for spatial narratives (setup → insight → call to action).
  • Integrate graphic design techniques (hierarchy, rhythm, visual anchors).
  • Emphasise accessibility and ethical communication in final outputs.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
1. Narrative structure
  2. Hook, context, insight, recommendation.
  3. Choosing the appropriate medium (static map, story map, slide deck).
  4. Design systems
  5. Grid-based layout, consistent typography, supporting graphics (charts, icons).
  6. Borrowing best practices from magazine spreads and infographics.
  7. Accessibility & inclusion
  8. Colour contrast testing, alternative text, accessible PDFs.
  9. Plain language summaries alongside visuals.
  10. Critique framework
  11. Provide rubric for peer review (clarity, accuracy, aesthetics, accessibility).
  12. Encourage iterative feedback loops.
