docs.title: Color Palettes Reference
docs.text: Consistent, accessible colors make your maps professional and readable. This guide covers creating palettes in QGIS and choosing colors for different map types.

docs.title: Example Color Palette
docs.text:
Here's an example palette showing typical colors for common map features. You should choose colors appropriate to your specific map and data:

Feature Example Color Hex Notes Water (ocean, lakes) Blue #4a90d9 Use blues for water—this is a universal convention Rivers, streams Light Blue #4fc3f7 Lighter blue for smaller water features Vegetation, forests Green #2e7d32 Darker greens for dense vegetation Parks, grassland Light Green #7cb342 Lighter greens for open land Urban areas Grey #455a64 Neutral greys for built-up areas Desert, bare ground Sand/Tan #d4a574 Warm earth tones Roads Brown/Grey #8d6e63 Depending on map style Points of interest Orange/Red #e65100 Warm colors draw attention

These are suggestions, not rules

Choose colors that work for your map and data. The key principles are:

  • Water should be blue — this is a strong cartographic convention
  • Vegetation should be green — another universal expectation
  • Use contrast — ensure features are distinguishable
  • Be consistent — use the same color for the same feature type across your maps

docs.title: Setting Up Your Palette in QGIS
Method 1: Settings → Options
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings ▶ Options ▶ Colors
  2. Click the green + button
  3. Enter hex code or use color picker
  4. Double-click to name the color (e.g., "Course - Deep Teal")
  5. Colors save automatically

docs.title: Method 2: From Any Color Selector
docs.text:
1. Click the dropdown arrow next to any color button
  2. Select Colors... to open the palette manager
  3. Add/edit colors as above

docs.title: Import/Export Palettes
docs.text:
Export: 

Settings → Options → Colors → ... → Export Colors
Save as .gpl file

Import: 

Settings → Options → Colors → ... → Import Colors
Select .gpl file

docs.title: Choosing Colors for Different Map Types
Categorical Maps (Categorized Symbology)
docs.text:
For distinct categories (land use, continents, zones):

  • Use qualitative color schemes with distinct hues
  • Avoid implying order (light→dark suggests ranking)
  • Maximum 7-8 distinct colors before confusion
  • Consider using patterns/hatching for additional distinction

Recommended: ColorBrewer Set2, Set3, Paired

docs.title: Sequential Maps (Graduated Symbology)
docs.text:
For numeric data showing progression (population, income):

  • Use sequential schemes: light→dark or single hue gradient
  • Lighter = lower values, Darker = higher values
  • 4-6 classes typically optimal

Recommended: ColorBrewer YlOrRd, Blues, Greens

docs.title: Diverging Maps
docs.text:
For data with meaningful midpoint (change, deviation from average):

  • Use diverging schemes: two hues meeting at neutral middle
  • Middle color = zero/average, extremes = positive/negative
  • Ensure equal visual weight on both sides

Recommended: ColorBrewer RdBu, PiYG, BrBG

docs.title: Color Vision Deficiency
docs.text:
~8% of males and ~0.5% of females have some form of color vision deficiency.

Do:

  • Use ColorBrewer schemes (designed for accessibility)
  • Add patterns/textures in addition to color
  • Test with a color blindness simulator
  • Ensure sufficient contrast between adjacent colors

Don't:

  • Rely solely on red/green distinction
  • Use rainbow color schemes for sequential data
  • Assume everyone sees colors the same way

docs.title: Safe Color Combinations
docs.text: Good Avoid Blue + Orange Red + Green Purple + Yellow Blue + Purple (similar) Teal + Coral Green + Brown Black + Yellow Red + Brown

docs.title: ColorBrewer Integration
docs.text: ColorBrewer provides research-backed color schemes.

docs.title: Using ColorBrewer in QGIS
docs.text:
1. Open Layer Properties → Symbology
  2. Click the Color ramp dropdown
  3. Select All Color Ramps → ColorBrewer
  4. Choose from:
  5. Sequential: Blues, Greens, YlOrRd, etc.
  6. Diverging: RdBu, PiYG, PRGn, etc.
  7. Qualitative: Set2, Paired, Dark2, etc.

docs.title: Creating Custom ColorBrewer Ramp
docs.text:
1. Visit colorbrewer2.org
  2. Select number of classes and scheme type
  3. Copy hex codes
  4. In QGIS: Color ramp → Create New → Catalog: cpt-city
  5. Or manually create gradient using hex codes

docs.title: Quick Reference: Map Type → Color Scheme
docs.text: Map Type Data Scheme Type Example Palettes Land use categories Categorical Qualitative Set2, Paired Population density Numeric, sequential Sequential YlOrRd, Blues Income levels Numeric, sequential Sequential Greens, PuBu Temperature change Diverging from 0 Diverging RdBu, coolwarm Election results Two categories Diverging RdBu (red/blue) Elevation/terrain Continuous Sequential terrain, dem NDVI (vegetation) -1 to +1 Diverging RdYlGn

docs.title: Saving Layer Styles
docs.text:
Once you've perfected a symbology:

  1. Right-click layer → Export → Save as QGIS Layer Style File
  2. Save as .qml file
  3. Reapply anytime: Right-click → Styles → Load Style

This saves colors, classification, labels—everything.

docs.title: Continuing Education Guide
docs.text: You've built a strong GIS foundation. Here's how to keep growing after the course ends.

docs.title: 1. Organize Your Course Work
docs.text:
• Create a portfolio folder with your best maps
  • Document your capstone project thoroughly
  • Back up all projects to cloud storage
  • Update LinkedIn with new GIS skills

docs.title: 2. Set a Practice Goal
docs.text:
The 30-day challenge: Complete one small GIS task per week for the next month.

Ideas:

  • Map your daily commute routes
  • Visualize local election results
  • Analyze walkability in your neighborhood
  • Map points of interest for a hobby (hiking trails, coffee shops, etc.)

Skills rust without use. Regular practice, even small projects, maintains proficiency.

docs.title: Final Advice
docs.text:
1. Practice regularly - Weekly mapping keeps skills sharp
  2. Build a portfolio - Documented projects matter more than certificates
  3. Join a community - Learning is faster with peers
  4. Teach others - Explaining concepts deepens understanding
  5. Stay curious - The best GIS practitioners never stop learning

Your GIS journey has just begun. Welcome to the community.

docs.title: Week 4 — Flood Risk Assessment
docs.text:
Sources: ELVIS (Australia) or USGS EarthExplorer (global)

Study area: Hawkesbury-Nepean floodplain (west of Sydney)

  • Bounding box: approximately 150.6°E to 150.85°E, 33.65°S to 33.45°S

  • Keep it small (~20km × 20km) for faster processing

  • Identified study area on ELVIS map

  • Downloaded DEM tiles for Hawkesbury-Nepean region
  • Extracted any ZIP files
  • Downloaded SA2 boundaries for study area (from Week 3 or ABS)
  • Files in week04/data/raw/:
    • DEM raster file(s) (.tif or similar)
    • SA2 boundaries (for zonal statistics)

docs.title: Week 5 — Crime Case Study
docs.text:

  • Extracted any ZIP files
  • Files in week05/data/raw/:

docs.title: Week 7 — Bridge to Python
docs.text:
No data download required!

  • Python environment set up (see Python Setup)
  • Created week07/ folder with data/raw/ and data/processed/
  • Notebook downloads sample data automatically

docs.title: Week 8 — Python Vector Workflows
docs.text:
No download needed! The notebook automatically downloads NYC sample data.

  • Run the notebook — it downloads NYC neighbourhoods + 311 complaints automatically

Optional: Use your own data

To use Australian data instead, export from QGIS and place in week08/data/raw/: - [ ] neighbourhoods.geojson (from Week 3) - [ ] incidents.geojson (from Week 5)

docs.title: Week 9 — Flood Risk (Python)
docs.text:
No download needed! The notebook fetches elevation data from Planetary Computer API.

  • Run the notebook — it downloads Copernicus DEM automatically
  • If API is unavailable, notebook falls back to synthetic terrain data

What the notebook downloads automatically:

  • Copernicus DEM 30m for Hawkesbury-Nepean region
  • SA2 boundaries (same study area as Week 4 QGIS)

Optional: Use your own study area

To analyze a different region, modify the bounding box in the notebook: 

bbox = [west, south, east, north]  # in decimal degrees

docs.text:
No data download required!

  • Notebook downloads street network from OpenStreetMap automatically
  • (Optional) Created facilities.geojson with custom locations

docs.title: Map Design Principles
docs.text: This guide introduces graphic design fundamentals that make maps effective. The same principles used in magazines, websites, and professional publications apply to cartography.

docs.title: Essential Map Elements
docs.text:
A map without these elements is incomplete

Every finished map must include these six elements. Missing any one makes your map invalid for professional or academic submission.

Element Purpose Where to place Title Tells viewers what the map shows Top of layout, largest text Legend Explains symbols and colors Right side or bottom, near map Scale bar Shows distance relationships Bottom of map frame North arrow Shows map orientation Top-right or bottom-right corner Data source Credits data providers, ensures trust Bottom of layout, small text Author & date Establishes responsibility and currency Bottom of layout with source

docs.title: Why Each Element is Required
docs.text:
Element Without it... Title Viewers don't know what they're looking at Legend Colors and symbols are meaningless Scale bar Distances cannot be understood North arrow Orientation is unknown Data source Map lacks credibility and violates attribution requirements Author/date No accountability; unclear if information is current

No exceptions for the core four

Title, Legend, Scale bar, and North arrow must appear on every map. A map missing any of these will not be accepted for submission.

docs.title: Pre-Export Checklist
docs.text:
Before exporting any map, verify:

  • Title — Clear, descriptive, answers "what is this map showing?"
  • Legend — All symbols explained, no unexplained colors
  • Scale bar — Appropriate units (km for large areas, m for local)
  • North arrow — Visible, unobtrusive, correctly oriented
  • Data source — All datasets credited
  • Author/date — Your name and creation date

docs.title: Why design matters
docs.text:
A map isn't just data—it's a visual argument. Good design helps your audience:

  • Understand the message quickly
  • Know where to look first
  • Trust the information
  • Remember the key points

Bad design creates confusion, even when the analysis is excellent.

docs.title: The grid system
docs.text: Professional designers don't place elements randomly. They use an invisible grid to create order and alignment.

docs.title: How grids work
docs.text:
Elements snap to column boundaries:

Element Columns Width Title 1–9 75% of page Main map 1–8 67% of page Legend 9–11 25% of page Credits 1–12 Full width

In this example: - Title spans 9 of 12 columns - Map takes 8 columns (2/3 of the page) - Legend takes 3 columns (1/4 of the page) - Credits span the full width

Magazine example: Open any magazine. Notice how headlines, images, and text align to invisible vertical lines. That's a grid.

For maps: Use a 12-column grid. Elements snap to column edges, creating visual order even when viewers don't consciously notice it.

docs.title: Gutters
docs.text:
The spaces between columns are called gutters. They prevent elements from touching and give the eye room to move.

  • Standard gutter: 5mm
  • Larger gutters (10mm) for more breathing room

docs.title: Visual hierarchy
docs.text: Hierarchy controls what viewers see first, second, third. Without it, everything competes for attention.

docs.title: The tools of hierarchy
docs.text: Tool How it works Map example Size Larger = more important Title bigger than legend text Color Bright/saturated = attention Red for key features, grey for context Position Top-left gets read first Title at top, credits at bottom Contrast High contrast = focal point Dark text on light background Isolation Surrounded by space = important Main map has margins around it

docs.title: The squint test
docs.text:
Squint at your map. What do you see?

  • The blurry shapes that stand out are your visual hierarchy
  • If everything blurs together equally, you have no hierarchy
  • If the wrong thing stands out, adjust size/color/position

docs.title: Balance
docs.text: A balanced layout feels stable. An unbalanced layout feels uncomfortable (even if viewers can't say why).

docs.title: Symmetrical vs asymmetrical
docs.text:
SymmetricalAsymmetrical Left Center Right 🗺️ MAP Legend

Everything centered on the page. Simple but static.

Map Area (2/3) Legend (1/3) 🗺️ MAP Legend

Heavier on left, balanced by legend on right. More dynamic and professional.

Asymmetrical balance is more dynamic and professional. Balance a large element (map) with smaller elements (legend, title) on the opposite side.

docs.title: Visual weight
docs.text:
Different elements have different "weights":

  • Large elements are heavy
  • Dark elements are heavier than light
  • Complex/detailed areas feel heavier than simple areas
  • Isolation makes elements feel heavier

Balance the weights across your page.

docs.title: Negative space (white space)
docs.text: Negative space is the empty area around and between elements. Beginners fill every inch; professionals use emptiness strategically.

docs.title: What negative space does
docs.text:
• Separates elements without needing boxes or lines
  • Creates breathing room so the eye can rest
  • Emphasizes importance — isolation draws attention
  • Improves readability — text needs margins

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Filling every corner Feels cluttered, overwhelming Remove or shrink non-essential elements Legend touching map Elements compete Add 10mm margin between Text to edge Feels cramped Maintain 15mm page margins Equal spacing everywhere Nothing stands out Vary spacing to group related items

docs.title: The "remove one thing" rule
docs.text: When your layout feels done, remove one element. If the map still works, leave it out. Repeat until removing anything would hurt the message.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
Elements that align feel intentional. Elements that almost align feel like mistakes.

Bad (ragged)Good (aligned) Element Position Title slightly left Map center-ish Legend far right Scale bar left of center Credits random indent

Left edges don't line up — looks accidental.

Element Position Title left edge Map left edge Legend left edge Scale bar left edge Credits left edge

Everything aligns to the same edge — looks intentional.

Rule: Pick alignment edges and stick to them. In QGIS, use guides or a grid.

docs.title: Contrast for readability
docs.text:
Text needs contrast ratio of 4.5:1 or higher against its background.

Good contrast Poor contrast Black on white Grey on white White on dark blue Yellow on white Dark text on light map Light text on busy map

Test: If you squint and the text disappears into the background, contrast is too low.

docs.title: Color for meaning
docs.text:
Colors aren't decoration—they carry meaning:

Color use Purpose Sequential (light→dark) Ordered data (low→high) Diverging (red←white→blue) Data with meaningful center Categorical (distinct hues) Different types (no order)

Limit colors: 3-5 colors maximum. More creates visual noise.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
Good map design uses all these principles:

Row Left (2/3) Right (1/3) Top 📰 TITLE — Large, high contrast Middle 🗺️ MAIN MAP 📋 LEGEND📏 Scale bar Bottom Data: ABS 2021 | CRS: EPSG:7856 | Author: Your Name Principle How it's applied Hierarchy Title is largest, at top position Balance Large map balanced by legend column Alignment All elements snap to grid columns Negative space Margins around edges, gutters between elements Grid 3-column structure, credits span full width

docs.title: Design critique rubric
docs.text: Use this during peer feedback sessions:

docs.title: 1. Clarity (Is the message clear?)
docs.text: Score Description 4 Message clear within 5 seconds 3 Message clear after 10-15 seconds 2 Requires explanation to understand 1 Unclear even with explanation

docs.title: 2. Visual hierarchy (Do you know where to look?)
docs.text: Score Description 4 Clear focal point, eye moves naturally 3 Mostly clear, minor competing elements 2 Multiple elements compete for attention 1 No clear hierarchy, chaotic

docs.title: 3. Technical accuracy
docs.text: Score Description 4 All labels correct, sources cited, scale accurate 3 Minor issues that don't affect interpretation 2 Notable errors causing confusion 1 Major errors undermining credibility

docs.title: 4. Accessibility
docs.text: Score Description 4 Works for colorblind viewers, good contrast, readable fonts 3 Minor accessibility issues 2 Some categories indistinguishable, text too small 1 Major barriers, unusable for many viewers

docs.title: Giving feedback
docs.text:
1. What works: "The graduated color scheme makes density patterns immediately clear."
  2. What could improve: "The legend overlaps part of the study area."
  3. Suggestion: "Move the legend to the empty ocean area in the lower right."

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Cartography Guide — Axis Maps
  • ColorBrewer — Color schemes for maps
  • Butterick's Practical Typography — Typography basics

docs.title: Layout Template Guide
docs.text: This guide teaches you to create professional map layouts in QGIS and save them as reusable templates. You'll learn the exact steps to build a layout once, then use it for every map you make.

docs.title: What is a layout template?
docs.text:
A layout template (.qpt file) saves your page setup, placeholders, and design elements—but not your map data. Think of it like a magazine template: the grid, fonts, and positions are set, but new content goes in each issue.

Benefits of templates: - Consistent look across all your maps - Faster production (no rebuilding from scratch) - Professional appearance - Forces good design habits

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Layout Manager
docs.text:
1. In QGIS, go to Project → Layout Manager
  2. Click Create... (or the blank page icon)
  3. Name your layout descriptively: A3_Landscape_Template
  4. Click OK

A new window opens—this is the Print Layout editor.

docs.title: Step 2: Set page size and orientation
docs.text:
1. Right-click on the blank page → Page Properties
  2. Or: Layout → Page Setup
  3. In the Item Properties panel (right side), set:
  4. Size: A3 (or A4 for smaller prints)
  5. Orientation: Landscape
  6. Your page dimensions appear:
Paper Size Width Height A3 landscape 420 mm 297 mm A4 landscape 297 mm 210 mm

docs.title: Part 2: Setting up guides and margins
docs.text: Guides create invisible alignment lines. Professional designers never place elements randomly—they snap to guides.

docs.title: Step 3: Add margin guides manually
docs.text:
1. Go to View → Manage Guides
  2. You'll see two tabs: Horizontal Guides and Vertical Guides

For A3 Landscape (420 × 297 mm) with 15mm margins:

Guide Type Click + and enter What it creates Horizontal 15 Top margin Horizontal 277 Bottom margin (297 − 20 for credits) Vertical 15 Left margin Vertical 405 Right margin (420 − 15)

Step-by-step:

  1. In the Guides panel, make sure you're on the Horizontal Guides tab
  2. Click the + button
  3. Type 15 and press Enter — this creates your top margin line
  4. Click + again, type 277 and press Enter — bottom margin line
  5. Switch to the Vertical Guides tab
  6. Click +, type 15 — left margin
  7. Click +, type 405 — right margin
  8. Close the Guides panel
  9. Enable View → Show Guides and View → Snap to Guides

You'll see dashed lines marking your safe area.

For A4 Landscape (297 × 210 mm):

Guide Type Position Horizontal 15 mm (top) Horizontal 190 mm (bottom, with 20mm for credits) Vertical 15 mm (left) Vertical 282 mm (right)

docs.title: Step 4: Add column guides (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
For a simple 3-zone layout (map + legend + margin):

  1. Add a vertical guide at 280 mm — this separates the map area from the legend area
Zone From To Width Left margin 0 15 mm 15 mm Map area 15 mm 280 mm 265 mm Legend area 280 mm 405 mm 125 mm Right margin 405 mm 420 mm 15 mm

docs.title: Part 3: Adding layout elements
docs.text: Now add the components that appear on every map.

docs.title: Step 5: Add the main map frame
docs.text:
1. Click Add Item → Add Map (or the map icon in toolbar)
  2. Draw a rectangle in the main area of your layout
  3. Position it precisely in Item Properties:

  4. Position and size:

    • X: 15 mm (left margin)
    • Y: 15 mm (top margin)
    • Width: 280 mm (leaves room for legend)
    • Height: 247 mm (accounts for top/bottom margins)

  5. Set map behaviour:

  6. Check Lock layers if you want specific layers visible
  7. Check Lock styles to preserve symbology
  8. Leave unchecked for flexible reuse

Tip: For templates, leave the map unlocked. When you reuse the template, click Set Map Extent to Match Main Canvas to show your current project.

docs.title: Step 6: Add a legend
docs.text:
1. Click Add Item → Add Legend
  2. Draw a rectangle to the right of the map frame
  3. In Item Properties:
  4. Position: X: 305 mm, Y: 50 mm

  5. Width: ~100 mm

  6. Configure legend settings:

  7. Uncheck Auto update (gives you control)
  8. Title: Leave blank or add "Legend"

  9. Fonts:

    • Title: 12 pt bold
    • Subgroup: 10 pt bold
    • Item: 9 pt regular

  10. Styling:

  11. Columns: 1 (or 2 for many items)
  12. Symbol width/height: 6 mm × 4 mm
  13. Spacing: Item space 2 mm

docs.title: Step 7: Add a scale bar
docs.text:
1. Click Add Item → Add Scale Bar
  2. Draw below or beside the map
  3. In Item Properties:
  4. Style: Single Box or Double Box
  5. Units: Meters or Kilometers (match your CRS)
  6. Segments: Left 0, Right 4
  7. Fixed width: 50 mm (or 100 mm for A3)
  8. Height: 3 mm

  9. Label: Every segment

  10. Position: bottom-left of map frame, inside the margin

docs.title: Step 8: Add a north arrow (required)
docs.text:
Every map needs a north arrow

A map without a north arrow is incomplete and will not be accepted for submission. Viewers must never have to guess which way is north.

  1. Click Add Item → Add North Arrow
  2. Draw a small box (15 × 15 mm)
  3. In Item Properties:
  4. Choose a simple SVG arrow (avoid ornate compass roses)

  5. Rotation: Sync with map (for rotated maps)

  6. Position: top-right or bottom-right corner of map frame

Style tips:

  • Keep it simple—a clean arrow is better than an ornate compass rose
  • Size: 10-20mm, visible but not dominant
  • Position consistently across all your maps (top-right or bottom-right)

docs.title: Step 9: Add title text
docs.text:
1. Click Add Item → Add Label
  2. Draw a text box at the top of your layout
  3. Enter placeholder text: [MAP TITLE]
  4. In Item Properties:
  5. Font: 24–32 pt, bold, sans-serif
  6. Horizontal alignment: Left or Center

  7. Vertical alignment: Middle

  8. Add a subtitle label below:

  9. Font: 14 pt, regular
  10. Text: [Subtitle or date]

docs.title: Step 10: Add credits/data sources
docs.text:
1. Add another label in the bottom margin
  2. Enter placeholder: Data: [SOURCE, YEAR] | CRS: [EPSG CODE] | Author: [NAME]
  3. In Item Properties:
  4. Font: 8–9 pt, regular
  5. Color: Dark grey (#333333)

docs.title: Step 11: Save the template file
docs.text:
1. Go to Layout → Save as Template...
  2. Navigate to your templates folder (create one if needed): 
    intro-gis/
└── templates/
    └── A3_landscape_standard.qpt
  3. Name it descriptively: A3_landscape_standard.qpt
  4. Click Save

The .qpt file contains: - Page size and orientation - All layout items (map frame, legend, scale bar, text boxes) - Positions and styling - Guide positions

It does not contain: - Your actual map data - Layer styles - Project settings

docs.title: Loading a template for a new map
docs.text:
1. Open your QGIS project with the map you want to export
  2. Go to Project → Layout Manager
  3. Click New from Template...
  4. Browse to your .qpt file
  5. Name the new layout: Week03_Choropleth_Map
  6. Click OK

docs.title: Updating the map content
docs.text:
1. Click on the map frame in your layout
  2. In Item Properties, click Set Map Extent to Match Main Canvas
  3. Or: Update Preview to refresh
  4. If layers changed, click Refresh in the Items panel

docs.title: Updating text placeholders
docs.text:
1. Click on each text label
  2. Replace placeholder text:
  3. [MAP TITLE] → Socioeconomic Disadvantage by SA2
  4. [Subtitle] → Greater Sydney, 2021
  5. [SOURCE, YEAR] → ABS Census 2021
  6. [EPSG CODE] → EPSG:7856
  7. [NAME] → Your Name

docs.title: Updating the legend
docs.text:
1. Click on the legend
  2. In Item Properties, click Update All to pull current layers
  3. Remove unwanted items: select → click minus button
  4. Rename items: double-click to edit text
  5. Reorder: drag items up/down

docs.title: Part 6: Template variations
docs.text: Create multiple templates for different purposes:

docs.title: Portrait template
docs.text:
• Size: A4 portrait (210 × 297 mm)
  • Map frame: Top 2/3 of page
  • Legend and text: Bottom 1/3
  • Good for: Reports, single-page handouts

docs.title: Comparison template
docs.text:
Two map frames side by side with shared legend below. Good for: Before/after, two time periods.

Layout:

┌─────────────────┬─────────────────┐
│                 │                 │
│    MAP 1        │    MAP 2        │
│    (2016)       │    (2021)       │
│                 │                 │
├─────────────────┴─────────────────┤
│           SHARED LEGEND           │
└───────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Dashboard template
docs.text:
Main map with inset maps and statistics. Good for: Executive summaries, presentations.

Layout:

┌───────────────────────┬───────────┐
│                       │  Legend   │
│      MAIN MAP         ├───────────┤
│                       │  Stats    │
├───────────┬───────────┼───────────┤
│  Inset 1  │  Inset 2  │  Notes    │
└───────────┴───────────┴───────────┘

docs.title: Quick reference: Layout toolbar
docs.text: Icon Tool Shortcut Add Map — Add Legend — Add Scale Bar — Add North Arrow — Add Label — Add Picture — Add Shape — Select/Move V Pan Layout P Zoom Z

docs.title: Common problems and fixes
docs.text: Problem Cause Solution Map shows wrong area Extent not updated Click Set Map Extent to Match Main Canvas Legend shows wrong layers Auto-update enabled Uncheck auto-update, manually select layers Scale bar shows wrong units CRS mismatch Check project CRS matches layout CRS Elements won't align Snapping off Enable View → Snap to Guides Template loads empty Normal behaviour Map frames are placeholders—update extent Text cut off Box too small Resize label box or reduce font size Blurry export Low DPI Export at 300 DPI for print

docs.title: For print (PDF)
docs.text:
• Resolution: 300 DPI
  • Format: PDF
  • Export → Export as PDF
  • Check: Print as raster if you have transparency issues

docs.title: For digital/web (PNG)
docs.text:
• Resolution: 150 DPI (or 96 for screen-only)
  • Format: PNG
  • Export → Export as Image
  • Choose PNG for transparency support

docs.title: For presentations
docs.text:
• Resolution: 150 DPI
  • Dimensions: 1920 × 1080 px (match your slides)
  • Export to PNG, then insert in PowerPoint/Google Slides

docs.title: Your template library
docs.text:
Over the course, build these templates:

  1. Week 2: A3_landscape_standard.qpt — Your main template
  2. Week 4: A3_terrain_with_hillshade.qpt — For raster/elevation maps
  3. Week 5: A3_comparison_two_maps.qpt — Side-by-side analysis
  4. Capstone: Customize for your project's specific needs

Save all templates in intro-gis/templates/ so they're easy to find.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
Before exporting, verify:

  • Map fills the frame appropriately (not too zoomed/too wide)
  • Legend matches visible layers (no extras, nothing missing)
  • Scale bar shows sensible numbers (not 17.3 km)
  • All placeholder text has been replaced
  • Fonts are readable at intended size
  • Elements align to guides
  • Data source and date are credited
  • Tested at 100% zoom—everything legible?

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:

  • Project Checklist — Full quality control list
  • QGIS Print Layout Documentation

docs.title: How to License Your Own Work
docs.text: When creating your own GIS projects, you'll need to choose licenses too. Here are some guidelines:

docs.title: If You Create Original Maps or Analyses
docs.text:
Recommended approach: - License your code under MIT (or another permissive license) - License your written content and visualizations under CC BY 4.0 - Document all data sources with their licenses

Example attribution for your work: 

Melbourne Bike Infrastructure Analysis
© 2025 [Your Name], CC BY 4.0

Code: MIT License
Data: City of Melbourne Open Data (CC BY 4.0)
      OpenStreetMap (ODbL)

docs.title: If You Combine Course Materials with Your Own Work
docs.text:
You can create derivative works that combine course materials with your additions:

Urban Heat Island Analysis for Sydney
Based on Introduction to GIS course materials © 2025 Claire Boulange (CC BY 4.0)
Extended analysis and additional data © 2025 [Your Name] (CC BY 4.0)

Data sources:
• NASA SRTM DEM (public domain)
• ABS ASGS boundaries (CC BY 4.0)
• [Your additional data sources]

docs.title: What About Data You Use?
docs.text:
Key principle: Data licenses are independent of code and content licenses.

  • Always preserve the original data license
  • Include proper attribution for all datasets
  • Document data sources in your README and map outputs
  • See the Data Inventory for examples of how to document data sources

Example data attribution in README: 

## Data Sources

| Dataset | Source | License | Access Date |
|---------|--------|---------|-------------|
| ABS SA2 Boundaries | Australian Bureau of Statistics | CC BY 4.0 | 2025-01-15 |
| SEIFA 2021 | Australian Bureau of Statistics | CC BY 4.0 | 2025-01-15 |
| Natural Earth Admin Boundaries | Natural Earth | Public domain | 2025-01-10 |

docs.title: MIT License Summary
docs.text:
You CAN: - Use the code commercially - Modify the code - Distribute copies - Sublicense the code - Use it privately

You MUST: - Include the original MIT license text - Include the copyright notice

You CANNOT: - Hold the author liable

docs.title: CC BY 4.0 Summary
docs.text:
You CAN: - Share (copy and redistribute) - Adapt (remix, transform, build upon) - Use commercially

You MUST: - Give appropriate credit (attribution) - Link to the license - Indicate if you made changes - Not suggest the licensor endorses you

You CANNOT: - Apply additional restrictions - Use technological measures to prevent others from doing what the license allows

docs.title: Can I use course materials for my capstone project?
docs.text: Yes! You can use code, adapt examples, and build on concepts from the course. Make sure to: - Attribute any code you adapt (MIT License) - Attribute any maps or written content you reuse (CC BY 4.0) - Add your own analysis and insights - Document your data sources separately

docs.title: Do I need permission to use course materials?
docs.text: No permission needed! Both licenses are permissive. Just provide proper attribution as described above.

docs.title: Can I use course materials in a commercial project?
docs.text: Yes, both MIT and CC BY 4.0 allow commercial use. Just maintain proper attribution.

docs.title: What if I only use a small snippet of code?
docs.text:
Even small snippets should include a brief attribution comment. For example:

# Buffer function adapted from intro-to-gis course (MIT License)
def create_buffer(gdf, distance):
    return gdf.buffer(distance)

docs.title: Can I translate the course materials?
docs.text:
Yes! CC BY 4.0 explicitly allows for translation. Include attribution and note that you created the translation:

Introduction to GIS course materials
© 2025 Claire Boulange, CC BY 4.0
Translated to [language] by [Your Name], [Year]

docs.title: What if I find an error and fix it?
docs.text: Please contribute back! You can: - Submit a pull request to the original repository - Or document your fixes with attribution if you're maintaining a fork

docs.title: How do I attribute multiple data sources?
docs.text:
List each source separately with its license. For example:

In a map footer: 

Data: ABS ASGS 2021 (CC BY 4.0) | Natural Earth (public domain) |
OpenStreetMap (ODbL) | Map design © 2025 [Your Name]

In a README: 

## Data Attribution

- ABS ASGS Edition 3 SA2 boundaries © Australian Bureau of Statistics, CC BY 4.0
- ABS SEIFA 2021 © Australian Bureau of Statistics, CC BY 4.0
- Natural Earth Admin Boundaries (public domain)
- OpenStreetMap data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL

docs.title: Can I remove the attribution from my maps?
docs.text: No—both CC BY 4.0 and individual data licenses require attribution. Design your map layout to include this information professionally (typically in a footer or text block).

docs.title: What about screenshots or screen recordings?
docs.text: If you create tutorials that show the course materials: - Attribute the original materials in your video description or accompanying text - Note that you're demonstrating the course content - Link to the original repository

docs.title: Do I need to license my student assignments?
docs.text: You own your work and can choose any license (or no license). However, if you build on course materials, you should attribute them regardless of what license you choose for your additions.

docs.title: What if I want to use stricter licensing?
docs.text: While you can license your original contributions under stricter terms, you cannot add restrictions to the course materials themselves—the CC BY 4.0 license prohibits this. Your new work can be more restrictive, but the course materials must remain under their original licenses.

docs.title: Common Scenarios
docs.text: What you're doing How to attribute Using code from a notebook Include copyright notice and MIT License reference in comments or README Adapting a course map design Include "Map design adapted from Introduction to GIS course materials © 2025 Claire Boulange, CC BY 4.0" in map footer Teaching with course slides Add attribution slide citing original course, author, and license Quoting lab instructions Use quotation marks and cite "Introduction to GIS course materials © 2025 Claire Boulange, CC BY 4.0" Building on course concepts Brief acknowledgment in README or documentation Using course datasets Attribute the original data source (see Data Inventory), not the course

docs.title: Writing Effective Map Titles
docs.text: A good title helps readers understand your map before they even look at the data. This guide covers title structure, common mistakes, and examples.

docs.title: The Title Formula
docs.text:
Structure: [What] + [Where] + [When] + optional [Why/So What]

Component Purpose Example What The phenomenon being mapped Population Density Where Geographic scope Greater Sydney When Time period of data 2021 Why/So What Interpretive hook (optional) Revealing Urban Sprawl Patterns

docs.title: Example 1: Demographic Map
docs.text:
Before After "Population Map" "Population Density in Greater Sydney, 2021" Better: "Uneven Growth: Population Density Shifts in Greater Sydney, 2016-2021"

Why it's better: Specific location, time period, and interpretive framing.

docs.title: Example 2: Transport Analysis
docs.text:
Before After "Bus Routes" "Public Transit Coverage in Melbourne's Western Suburbs" Better: "Transit Deserts: Areas Beyond 400m Walking Distance to Bus Stops, Melbourne West"

Why it's better: Specifies the phenomenon (coverage gaps), location, and implies the analytical finding.

docs.title: Example 3: Environmental Map
docs.text:
Before After "Flood Risk" "Flood-Prone Areas in Brisbane River Catchment" Better: "1-in-100 Year Flood Extent: Properties at Risk in Brisbane River Catchment, 2024 Update"

Why it's better: Specifies the flood scenario, what's at risk, and data currency.

docs.title: Example 4: Health Access
docs.text:
Before After "Healthcare Facilities" "Hospital Accessibility in Rural NSW" Better: "Beyond Reach: Populations More Than 30 Minutes from Emergency Care, Rural NSW"

Why it's better: Frames the issue (access gaps), specifies the threshold, and targets the affected group.

docs.title: 1. Too Vague
docs.text:
• "Land Use Map"
  • "Crime Analysis"
  • "Environmental Data"

Problem: Could apply to thousands of maps. Provides no useful information.

docs.title: 2. Too Technical
docs.text:
• "SEIFA IRSD Decile Quintiles by SA2"
  • "Kernel Density Estimation Output (h=500m)"

Problem: Jargon excludes non-specialist audiences. Define acronyms or use plain language.

docs.title: 3. Missing Context
docs.text:
• "Melbourne 2021"
  • "NSW Health Facilities"

Problem: What about Melbourne? What aspect of health facilities?

docs.title: 4. Too Long
docs.text:
• "A Comprehensive Analysis of the Spatial Distribution of Socioeconomic Disadvantage as Measured by the Australian Bureau of Statistics Index of Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage Across Statistical Area Level 2 Boundaries in Greater Melbourne for the 2021 Census Year"

Problem: Titles should fit on one line. Move details to subtitles or captions.

docs.title: Option 1: Descriptive (Neutral)
docs.text:
Format: [Topic] in [Location], [Date]

"Population Density in Greater Sydney, 2021"

Best for: Reference maps, technical reports, data documentation.

docs.title: Option 2: Interpretive (Engaging)
docs.text:
Format: [Insight]: [Specific Description]

"Urban Sprawl Accelerates: Population Growth Hotspots in Sydney's Outer Suburbs, 2016-2021"

Best for: Presentations, journalism, advocacy, storytelling.

docs.title: Option 3: Question-Based
docs.text:
Format: [Question the map answers]

"Where Are Melbourne's Transit Deserts?"

Best for: Exploratory analysis, community engagement, educational materials.

docs.title: Using Subtitles
docs.text:
For complex maps, use a main title plus subtitle:

Main title: Short, attention-grabbing (5-10 words)

Subtitle: Additional context, methods, or data source (10-20 words)

Example:

Uneven Recovery Employment Change by Suburb in Greater Brisbane, March 2020 to March 2023

docs.title: Title Checklist
docs.text:
Before finalizing your title, verify:

  • Specific: Could this title only apply to YOUR map?
  • Located: Is the geographic scope clear?
  • Dated: Is the time period specified?
  • Jargon-free: Would a non-specialist understand every word?
  • Accurate: Does the title match what the map actually shows?
  • Concise: Can it fit on one line at readable size?

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Map Type Title Template Choropleth "[Variable] in [Location], [Date]" Change map "[Variable] Change in [Location], [Start]-[End]" Hotspot analysis "[Phenomenon] Hotspots in [Location]" Accessibility "[Service] Access in [Location]: [Threshold] Analysis" Comparison "[Location A] vs [Location B]: [Variable Compared]"

docs.title: Test Your Title
docs.text:
Ask someone unfamiliar with your project:

  1. "Based on this title, what do you expect to see on the map?"
  2. "What's the main message or finding?"
  3. "Who do you think would find this map useful?"

If their answers match your intentions, your title works. If not, revise.

docs.title: Using Google Colab
docs.text:
Google Colab provides a free Python environment in your browser - no installation required.

First time setup:

  1. Click the "Open in Colab" button above
  2. Sign in with your Google account
  3. The notebook opens in a temporary environment

Installing packages:

Colab has many packages pre-installed, but you may need to add GIS libraries:

# Run this cell first in Colab
!pip install geopandas rasterio rasterstats osmnx contextily

Saving your work:

  • File → Save a copy in Drive to save to your Google Drive
  • File → Download → Download .ipynb to save locally

Limitations:

  • Sessions timeout after ~12 hours of inactivity
  • Large datasets may exceed free memory limits
  • Some packages may have version differences

  4. Open and run notebooks

Local setup gives you: - Faster performance - Full control over packages - Persistent storage - Offline access

docs.title: Project Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist throughout your GIS projects. Print it out or keep it open as you work.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
• Research question or objective is clearly defined
  • Study area boundaries identified
  • Required datasets listed with sources
  • Appropriate CRS selected for your region
  • Project timeline realistic for available time

docs.title: Workspace Setup
docs.text:
• Using the week-based folder structure: 
    intro-gis/
└── capstone/
    ├── data/
    │   ├── raw/        ← Original downloads (never edit!)
    │   └── processed/  ← Your cleaned/modified data
    ├── capstone.qgz    ← QGIS project file
    ├── notebooks/      ← Python analysis
    └── exports/        ← Your final maps
  • Data sources bookmarked or documented
  • Backup location identified (cloud/USB)

docs.title: Acquiring Data
docs.text:
• Downloaded from authoritative sources
  • Checked licensing allows your intended use
  • Recorded download date and version
  • Saved to data/raw/ folder (untouched originals)
  • Created README noting source URLs

docs.title: Organizing Data
docs.text:
• File names are lowercase, no spaces (use underscores)
  • File names include date or version where relevant
  • Related files kept together (shapefile components)
  • Processed data saved separately from raw data
  • Large unused files removed to save space

docs.title: Data Quality
docs.text:
• Checked for missing values or NULL geometries
  • Verified CRS matches project requirements
  • Confirmed attribute fields contain expected values
  • Checked for obvious errors (negative populations, etc.)
  • Documented any cleaning steps performed

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
• Saved as .qgz in your week or capstone folder
  • "Save paths: Relative" enabled (Project → Properties → General)
  • Project CRS set appropriately for study area
  • Project title filled in (Project → Properties → General)

docs.title: Layer Management
docs.text:
• Layer names are clear and descriptive (renamed from defaults)
  • Layers organized in logical groups
  • Unused layers removed from project
  • Layer order makes sense (points on top, polygons below)
  • All layers display without errors

docs.title: Styling & Symbology
docs.text:
• Colors chosen with purpose (not random defaults)
  • Color ramp appropriate for data type:
  • Sequential for ordered data (light→dark)
  • Diverging for data with meaningful middle
  • Qualitative for categories
  • Classification method documented (equal interval, quantiles, etc.)
  • Number of classes appropriate (usually 4-7)
  • Tested with colorblind simulator

docs.title: Essential Elements (all required)
docs.text:
• Title: Specific, includes What + Where + When
  • Legend: All symbols explained, units shown
  • Scale bar: Appropriate units, reasonable size
  • North arrow: Required on every map
  • Data sources: All datasets credited
  • Author & date: Your name and creation date

docs.title: Visual Quality
docs.text:
• Clear visual hierarchy (title largest, important features prominent)
  • Text readable at intended viewing size
  • Consistent fonts (max 2 font families)
  • White space used effectively
  • No overlapping labels
  • Borders and frames consistent

docs.title: Layout Polish
docs.text:
• All elements aligned properly
  • Margins consistent around edges
  • Legend doesn't obscure important map areas
  • Inset/locator map included if helpful
  • Color palette harmonious

docs.title: Color & Contrast
docs.text:
• Text contrast ratio ≥4.5:1 (use WebAIM checker)
  • Tested with Color Oracle for colorblind accessibility
  • Categories distinguishable without relying solely on color
  • Avoided red/green combinations for critical distinctions

docs.title: Typography
docs.text:
• Minimum 9pt for print, 12pt for digital display
  • Sans-serif fonts for labels (Arial, Open Sans, etc.)
  • Sufficient spacing between labels
  • Text buffers/halos improve readability on busy backgrounds

docs.title: Digital Distribution
docs.text:
• Alt text prepared describing the map
  • High contrast version available if needed
  • PDF tagged for accessibility (if submitting PDF)

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Methods appropriate for research question
  • Analysis steps documented and reproducible
  • Parameters and thresholds justified
  • Intermediate outputs spot-checked for errors
  • Results make logical sense

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Key patterns identified and described
  • Findings connected back to research question
  • Limitations honestly acknowledged
  • Alternative explanations considered
  • Conclusions proportional to evidence

docs.title: Spatial Statistics (if applicable)
docs.text:
If your project involves regression or statistical analysis:

  • Checked for spatial autocorrelation using Moran's I
  • If Moran's I significant, used spatial regression instead of OLS
  • Chose appropriate spatial model (lag vs error) with justification
  • Checked residuals for remaining spatial autocorrelation
  • Interpreted coefficients correctly (with uncertainty)
  • Reported model diagnostics (R², AIC, p-values)

Resources: Spatial Statistics reading | Spatial Statistics notebook

docs.title: File Preparation
docs.text:
• Exported at correct resolution:
  • Print: 300 DPI minimum
  • Web/presentation: 150 DPI or 1920×1080px
  • Social media: Platform-specific dimensions
  • Correct format:
  • PDF for print/archival
  • PNG for web (supports transparency)
  • JPG for photos/smaller files
  • File size reasonable for submission method
  • Test-opened file to verify it looks correct

docs.title: Final Checks
docs.text:
• Opened project fresh to verify layers load
  • Viewed export at 100% zoom—is everything readable?
  • Spell-checked all text elements
  • Verified all required components included
  • File named according to submission guidelines

docs.title: For Your Records
docs.text:
• Research question clearly stated
  • Data sources documented with URLs and dates
  • Methods described step-by-step
  • Key findings summarized (2-4 bullet points)
  • Limitations noted
  • Reflection completed

docs.title: For Reproducibility
docs.text:
• Someone else could recreate your analysis from notes
  • All files organized with clear names
  • README file explains folder contents
  • Processing steps documented in order

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text: Mistake How to Fix Missing scale bar Always include—Layout → Add Scale Bar Legend doesn't match map Regenerate legend after symbology changes Unreadable text Increase font size, add text buffer No data sources Credit every dataset in the map margin Broken layer paths Use relative paths, keep folder structure Wrong file version Include date/version in filename Cluttered map Simplify—remove unnecessary elements Poor color choices Use ColorBrewer, test for accessibility CRS mismatch Set project CRS, reproject layers if needed Missing metadata Document source, date, license for all data

docs.title: Quick Reference: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Action Windows/Linux macOS Save project Ctrl+S Cmd+S Undo Ctrl+Z Cmd+Z Pan map Hold Space + drag Hold Space + drag Zoom in/out Scroll wheel Scroll wheel Select features Click or drag box Click or drag box Open attribute table F6 F6 Identify features Ctrl+Shift+I Cmd+Shift+I

docs.title: Submission Checklist
docs.text:
Final verification before you submit:

  • All required files present
  • Files named correctly per guidelines
  • Project/maps open without errors
  • Exports are readable and complete
  • Documentation/reflection included
  • Submitted to correct location
  • Backup copy saved for yourself

You're ready to submit!

docs.title: QGIS Quickstart Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Use this page during Week 1 to verify your setup and revisit essential workflows throughout the course.

docs.title: Launch & project setup
docs.text:
• Open QGIS LTR 3.34.x (course-approved version).
  • Create workspace folders: data/, projects/, exports/, screenshots/, notes/.
  • Start a new project (Project ▶ New) and set the project CRS to EPSG:4326 unless instructed otherwise.
  • Save the project as projects/week01_orientation.qgz, ensuring Save paths relative to project is checked.

docs.title: Essential panels
docs.text:
Panel Toggle Purpose Browser View ▶ Panels ▶ Browser Browse local folders or services. Layers View ▶ Panels ▶ Layers Manage layer order and visibility. Processing Toolbox View ▶ Panels ▶ Processing Toolbox Access geoprocessing tools. Layer Styling View ▶ Panels ▶ Layer Styling Apply symbology, labels, formatting.

Arrange Browser on the left and Layers on the right for quick drag-and-drop.

docs.title: Add data
docs.text:
• Vector: Drag shapefile/GeoPackage from Browser onto the map.
  • CSV with coordinates: Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Delimited Text Layer… → set X = longitude, Y = latitude, CRS = EPSG:4326.
  • Raster: Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Raster Layer… or drag GeoTIFFs directly.

docs.title: Attribute table essentials
docs.text:
• Right-click a layer → Open Attribute Table.
  • Use Select Features to highlight records.
  • Field Calculator adds new columns (e.g., area($geometry)).
  • Toggle editing (pencil icon) before modifying attributes.

docs.title: Symbology & labels
docs.text:
1. Select a layer and open Layer Styling.
  2. Symbology: choose Single, Graduated (numeric), or Categorised (text).
  3. Labels: enable Single Labels, choose attribute, use data-defined overrides for scale-based visibility.

docs.title: Export a map layout
docs.text:
1. Project ▶ New Print Layout… → name it.
  2. Add map frame, title, legend, scale bar via the Add Item menu.
  3. Export as PNG/PDF/SVG to the exports/ folder.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
• Ctrl/Cmd + L — Open Data Source Manager.
  • Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F — Toggle full screen.
  • Ctrl/Cmd + P — Print Layout manager.
  • Ctrl/Cmd + 1/2/3 — Map/List/Table views in Attribute Table.
  • Hold Space — Temporarily pan when digitising.

Adjust shortcuts via Settings ▶ Keyboard Shortcuts.

docs.title: Troubleshooting quick fixes
docs.text: Issue Solution Missing panels Re-enable under View ▶ Panels, or reset UI (Settings ▶ Options ▶ System ▶ Reset). Slow rendering Pause rendering (Render toggle button) or enable simplification (Settings ▶ Options ▶ Rendering). CRS mismatch Check layer CRS (Layer ▶ Properties ▶ Source); reproject with Vector ▶ Data Management Tools ▶ Reproject Layer. Plugin errors Disable non-essential plugins until core workflows are stable.

docs.title: Useful links
docs.text:
• QGIS Training Manual: https://docs.qgis.org/latest/en/docs/training_manual/
  • Keyboard shortcuts reference: Help ▶ Keyboard Shortcuts Reference
  • Course onboarding: Install QGIS, Downloading datasets

docs.title: Reflection Prompts
docs.text: Use these prompts to capture weekly takeaways, blockers, and questions. Copy them into your notes or version-controlled journal.

docs.title: Week 1 — QGIS Orientation
docs.text:
• What worked well during installation and first project setup?
  • Where do you still feel unsure navigating the QGIS interface?
  • List any issues to raise during the support clinic.

docs.title: Week 2 — Symbology & Layouts
docs.text:
• Which design choices (colour, labelling, layout) are you most proud of?
  • How will you iterate on accessibility for the next map export?
  • What questions remain about the styling tools or print composer?

docs.title: Week 3 — Vector Analysis & Joins
docs.text:
• Which attribute or spatial query unlocked the most insight this week?
  • How confident do you feel using the Field Calculator and selections?
  • Note any datasets you plan to bring into the crime case study.

docs.title: Week 4 — Raster & Terrain
docs.text:
• What raster styling or analysis technique felt most approachable?
  • Where do you still need support with reprojection or interpolation?
  • Capture ideas for applying these techniques to environmental resilience topics.

docs.title: Week 5 — Crime Mapping
docs.text:
• How did hotspot tools change your understanding of the data?
  • What contextual information would make your map more actionable?
  • List follow-up tasks to refine temporal filters or storytelling elements.

docs.title: Week 6 — Public Health & Accessibility
docs.text:
• Which network or service-area insight felt most meaningful for equity analysis?
  • Document any friction encountered with plugins or data availability.
  • Identify questions to bring into the Python bridge regarding reproducibility.

docs.title: Week 7 — Bridge to Python
docs.text:
• What part of the managed environment setup was clearest, and what needs clarification?
  • How ready do you feel to translate QGIS habits into scripted workflows?
  • List dependencies or datasets you want packaged before diving into Python.

docs.title: Week 8 — Python Vector Workflows
docs.text:
• Which step translated most naturally from QGIS into Python?
  • Where did Python automation save you time or introduce complexity?
  • List questions to bring to the reproducibility clinic next session.

docs.title: Week 9 — Raster & Remote Sensing in Python
docs.text:
• How well did the raster workflows translate from QGIS into code?
  • What questions remain about band math, masking, or zonal statistics?
  • Capture automation ideas to bring into the capstone project.

docs.title: Week 10 — Transport Networks
docs.text:
• Which part of the network pipeline felt most valuable?
  • Note any data gaps or assumptions that could impact conclusions.
  • Identify enhancements to test before Week 11’s design studio.

docs.title: Week 11 — Design & Storytelling
docs.text:
• What feedback did you receive on layout, typography, or narrative flow?
  • How will you adapt your map for accessibility (colour contrast, alt text, annotations)?
  • List final tasks required to polish your capstone deliverables.

docs.text:

docs.title: QGIS Toolbar Reference
docs.text: Keep this reference handy when arranging QGIS panels in Weeks 1–2.

docs.title: Recommended layout
docs.text:
• Top menu: Project, File, Edit, View, Layer, Plugins, Vector, Raster.
  • Toolbar order (left → right):
  • Project (New, Open, Save)
  • Map Navigation (Pan, Zoom In/Out, Zoom Full, Zoom to Layer)
  • Attributes (Identify, Select by Rectangle/Polygon/Freehand)
  • Digitizing (Toggle Editing, Add Feature, Move Feature)
  • Snapping (Snapping On/Off, Snapping Options)
  • View/Measure (Measure Line/Area, Overview)
  • Plugin shortcuts (Value Tool, QuickMapServices when enabled)

Drag toolbars using the dotted handle on their left edge. Collapse infrequently used toolbars to the side to reduce clutter.
