docs.title: Week 1 · QGIS Orientation & Project Setup
docs.text: Welcome to your GIS journey! This week you'll set up your workspace, navigate the QGIS interface, and create your first map. By the end of this session, you'll have a working QGIS installation, an organized project folder structure, and hands-on experience loading and styling spatial data. Think of this week as building your foundation—everything that follows builds on these core skills.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you'll be able to:

  1. Install QGIS (LTR 3.34 recommended) and configure your workspace.
  2. Navigate the QGIS interface (Browser, Layers, Processing Toolbox, Layout Manager).
  3. Load vector layers, inspect attribute tables, and apply basic symbology.
  4. Create a custom color palette for consistent map styling throughout the course.
  5. Build a print layout with title, legend, scale bar, and data credits.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Follow the Install QGIS guide and confirm the app launches
  • Review the lecture: Foundations of GIS
  • Read the GIS primer: Understanding GIS

Data downloads happen in class

We'll download Natural Earth datasets together during class. Your facilitator will guide you through the process—no pre-class downloads required!

docs.title: Activity 1: Confirm your QGIS installation
docs.text:
Let's make sure QGIS is properly installed and your workspace is organized.

Steps:

  1. Launch QGIS and confirm you see the welcome screen
  2. Check the version: Help ▶ About — you should see QGIS 3.34 LTR (or newer)
  3. Enable key panels if they're not visible:
  4. View ▶ Panels ▶ Browser Panel
  5. View ▶ Panels ▶ Layers Panel
  6. View ▶ Panels ▶ Processing Toolbox
  7. If your interface looks cluttered, reset it: Settings ▶ Options ▶ System ▶ Reset user interface

Save your layout

Once you've arranged panels the way you like, QGIS remembers your preferences. Spend a few minutes getting comfortable with the layout now—it'll save time later.

docs.title: Activity 2: Set up your project workspace
docs.text:
Organized files make everything easier. You'll create a folder structure that you'll use throughout the course.

Steps:

  1. Create a course folder (e.g., GIS_Course or intro-to-gis) in a location you can easily find
  2. Inside that folder, create these subfolders:
  3. data/raw — original downloaded datasets (never edit these)
  4. data/processed — cleaned and filtered data you create
  5. projects — your QGIS project files (.qgz)
  6. exports — maps, images, and outputs you create
  7. screenshots — helpful for documentation and assignments
  8. Navigate to this folder in QGIS's Browser Panel to confirm it appears

Why this structure?

Keeping raw data separate from processed data helps you trace your steps. If something goes wrong, you can always return to the original data and start fresh.

docs.title: Activity 3: Create and configure your first project
docs.text:
Now you'll create a QGIS project file and set some important defaults.

Steps:

  1. Create a new project: Project ▶ New (or Ctrl/Cmd + N)
  2. Set the project CRS (Coordinate Reference System):
  3. Click the CRS button in the bottom-right corner (shows something like EPSG:4326)
  4. Search for 4326 (this is WGS 84, a common global CRS)
  5. Select it and click OK

What is CRS?

CRS tells QGIS how to interpret coordinates. Think of it like a language for locations—"EPSG:4326" means coordinates are in latitude/longitude degrees (like GPS). We'll cover this in depth in Week 2. For now, just use 4326 for global data.

  1. Enable relative paths (makes your project portable):
  2. Project ▶ Properties ▶ General
  3. Check "Save paths: Relative"
  4. Click OK
  5. Save the project:
  6. Project ▶ Save As...
  7. Navigate to your projects/ folder
  8. Name it week01_orientation.qgz
  9. Click Save

docs.title: Activity 4: Load your first spatial data
docs.text:
Time to see some geography! You'll load Natural Earth country boundaries and explore the attribute table.

Steps:

  1. In the Browser Panel, navigate to where you saved your Natural Earth data
  2. Find the file ne_110m_admin_0_countries.shp
  3. Drag it onto the map canvas (or double-click it)
  4. You should see a world map appear with country outlines
  5. Right-click the layer in the Layers Panel → Open Attribute Table
  6. Explore the table:
  7. Click column headers to sort (try sorting by POP_EST for population)
  8. Notice fields like NAME, CONTINENT, GDP_MD, etc.
  9. Each row represents one country
  10. Close the attribute table

Understanding the connection

Use the Identify Features tool to click on any country and see its data:

  1. Find the icon in the toolbar
  2. Click the icon to activate the tool (your cursor changes)
  3. Click on any country on the map
  4. A panel appears showing that country's attributes (name, population, etc.)

This shows how the map and table are linked—each shape on the map is connected to a row of data.

Optional: Load the Admin 1 layer (ne_110m_admin_1_states_provinces.shp) to see states and provinces. Notice how it adds more detail.

docs.title: Activity 5: Apply basic symbology
docs.text:
Let's make the map more meaningful by coloring countries by continent.

Steps:

  1. Right-click your countries layer → Properties → Symbology tab
  2. At the top, change Single Symbol to Categorized
  3. Set Value to CONTINENT
  4. Click Classify (this creates a color for each continent)
  5. Click OK to apply
  6. Your map should now show different colors for each continent

Symbology types explained

Type Use for Example Single Symbol All features look the same All countries in blue Categorized Text/category data Different color per continent Graduated Numeric data Darker colors for higher population

The Classify button tells QGIS to scan your data and create groups automatically.

Experiment: Try changing it to Graduated symbology using POP_EST (population) to see countries colored by population ranges.

Week 2 preview

Next week you'll dive deeper into color choices, classification methods, and cartographic design principles. For now, just get comfortable with the mechanics.

docs.title: Activity 6: Create a course color palette
docs.text:
Consistent colors make your maps look professional. QGIS lets you save custom colors for easy reuse throughout the course.

Steps:

  1. Open the color picker:
  2. Go to Settings ▶ Options ▶ Colors tab

  3. Or: When in any color selector, click the dropdown arrow → Colors...

  4. Add colors to your palette:

  5. Click the green + button to add a new color
  6. Use the color wheel or enter hex codes
  7. Here are some example colors to get you started:
Feature Example Hex Notes Water #4a90d9 Blues for water (cartographic convention) Vegetation #2e7d32 Greens for forests/parks Highlights #e65100 Warm colors draw attention Urban #455a64 Neutral greys Rivers #4fc3f7 Lighter blue for streams
  1. Label your colors:
  2. Double-click on a color swatch
  3. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., "Course - Water Teal")

  4. Adding "Course -" prefix keeps them grouped together

  5. Access your palette anytime:

  6. In any color picker, your custom colors appear under Recent Colors or Standard Colors
  7. The palette saves automatically with your QGIS profile

Import/export palettes

You can export your palette to share with classmates:

  • In the Colors tab, click ... → Export Colors
  • Save as .gpl (GIMP palette) file
  • Share the file; others import via Import Colors

Why this matters:

  • Consistency: Same colors across all 12 weeks = professional portfolio
  • Efficiency: No searching for "that blue I used last time"
  • Accessibility: Plan accessible colors once, use them everywhere

ColorBrewer for map-specific palettes

For choropleth maps (graduated colors), use ColorBrewer to generate accessible, sequential or diverging palettes. You'll practice this in Week 2.

docs.title: Activity 7: Create your first layout
docs.text:
A layout is how you turn your QGIS canvas into a polished map ready for export or printing.

Steps:

  1. Create a new layout: Project ▶ New Print Layout...
  2. Give it a name (e.g., "World Map") and click OK
  3. A new window opens—this is your layout canvas (a blank page)

Finding the layout tools

The layout window has its own toolbar on the left side. Key tools:

Icon Tool What it does Add Map Inserts your map canvas Add Label Adds text (titles, credits) Add Legend Adds map legend Add Scale Bar Adds scale reference Add North Arrow Shows map orientation (required!)

Hover over any icon in QGIS to see its name.

  1. Add a map:
  2. Click the Add Map button in the toolbar
  3. Draw a rectangle on the canvas (click and drag to define the area)

  4. Your map from the main QGIS window appears in this frame

  5. Add a title:

  6. Click the Add Label button
  7. Draw a box at the top of the page
  8. In the panel on the right, find the text box (shows "Lorem ipsum" as placeholder text)
  9. Delete the placeholder and type your title: "World Countries by Continent"
  10. Scroll down in the panel to find Font settings → increase size to 18-24pt
  11. Add a legend:
  12. Click the Add Legend button
  13. Draw a box where you want the legend
  14. In Legend properties, you can rename items or remove unnecessary entries
  15. Add a scale bar:
  16. Click the Add Scale Bar button
  17. Draw a box at the bottom of your map
  18. Add a north arrow:
  19. Click Add Item → Add North Arrow (or find the compass icon in the toolbar)
  20. Draw a small box in the top-right or bottom-right corner
  21. Choose a simple arrow style

North arrow is required

Every map must have a north arrow. A map without one is incomplete and will not be accepted for submission.

  1. Add data source:
  2. Add another label at the bottom: "Source: Natural Earth, 2024"
  3. Export your map:
  4. Click Layout ▶ Export as Image... (or Export as PDF)
  5. Save to exports/week01_first_map.png

Practice makes perfect

Layouts can feel fiddly at first. Don't worry about making it perfect—you'll get lots of practice in Week 2.

docs.title: QGIS won't launch or crashes on startup
docs.text:
• Mac: Right-click the app → Open (bypasses Gatekeeper security warning the first time)
  • Windows: Run as Administrator if you get permission errors
  • All platforms: Delete the QGIS user profile folder to reset settings:
  • Windows: C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Roaming\QGIS\QGIS3\
  • Mac: ~/Library/Application Support/QGIS/QGIS3/
  • Linux: ~/.local/share/QGIS/QGIS3/

docs.title: Layer doesn't appear on the map
docs.text:
• Check visibility: Is the checkbox ticked in the Layers panel?
  • Check layer order: Drag layers up/down—polygons should be below points
  • Zoom to layer: Right-click layer → Zoom to Layer to find it
  • Check CRS: If the layer is in a different CRS, it may appear in the wrong location. Right-click → Properties → Source to see the CRS

docs.title: "Layer is not valid" error when adding data
docs.text:
• File path issue: Move files out of folders with special characters or spaces
  • Missing components: Shapefiles need all companion files (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj) in the same folder
  • Corrupted download: Re-download the file

docs.title: Attribute table is empty or shows wrong data
docs.text:
• Check the right layer: Make sure you opened the correct layer's attribute table
  • Encoding issue: Try Layer Properties ▶ Source ▶ Data source encoding → change to UTF-8

docs.title: Can't find a tool or panel
docs.text:
• Panels: View ▶ Panels → check the panel you need
  • Toolbars: View ▶ Toolbars → check the toolbar you need
  • Processing Toolbox: Processing ▶ Toolbox or press Ctrl+Alt+T
  • Reset interface: Settings ▶ Options ▶ System ▶ Reset user interface to default

docs.title: Project won't save or gives errors
docs.text:
• Invalid path: Avoid special characters in folder/file names
  • Permissions: Make sure you have write access to the folder
  • Relative paths: Check Project ▶ Properties ▶ General ▶ Save paths is set to "Relative"

docs.title: Support materials
docs.text:
• Slides: Week 01 lecture deck
  • Reading: Understanding GIS
  • Cheat sheet: QGIS Quickstart
  • Dataset checklist: Week 1 items

docs.title: Reflect
docs.text:
Take 10 minutes to answer these questions in your Week 1 reflection:

  • What was one thing that went smoothly during setup?
  • What was one challenge you encountered? How did you solve it (or what do you still need help with)?
  • What surprised you most about QGIS or spatial data?
  • What's one keyboard shortcut or panel arrangement that you want to remember?

Keep notes

Recording your successes and struggles helps you troubleshoot later and makes it easier to help classmates. Your reflection is also valuable for your own learning—you'll look back and see how far you've come!

docs.title: What you'll submit
docs.text:
• QGIS project file: projects/week01_orientation.qgz with Natural Earth layers loaded and styled
  • Exported map: exports/week01_first_map.png (or PDF) showing your categorized world map
  • Your Week 1 reflection entry

Map submission requirements

Your exported map must include these four elements or it will not be accepted:

  • Title — What the map shows
  • Legend — What the colors/symbols mean
  • Scale bar — Distance reference
  • North arrow — Map orientation

See Map Design Principles for the complete checklist.

docs.title: Coming up next week
docs.text: Week 2 focuses on advanced symbology, labelling, and professional layout design. You'll learn about color theory, classification methods, and cartographic conventions. Bring a map you admire (digital or printed) to share during the Week 2 design show-and-tell—we'll discuss what makes effective maps work.

docs.title: Week 2 · Symbology, Labelling & Layouts
docs.text: A map is more than just data on a canvas—it's a communication tool. This week, you'll learn how to make intentional design choices that guide your audience's eye, tell clear stories, and make your maps accessible to diverse audiences. You'll master advanced symbology techniques, create intelligent labels, and assemble polished layouts that look professional.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you'll be able to:

  1. Apply graduated, categorised, and rule-based symbology to communicate spatial patterns.
  2. Configure labels with data-driven styling and scale-dependent rules.
  3. Design an export-ready layout using cartographic design principles (hierarchy, balance, accessibility).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Reopen your Week 1 project and ensure Natural Earth layers load correctly
  • Bring an inspirational map to share (digital or printed)—note one design element you appreciate
  • Review the lecture: Cartographic Conventions & Colour
  • Skim the Layout Template guide for reference

Data downloads happen in class

We'll download the renewable energy and world cities datasets together during class. Your facilitator will guide you through the process.

docs.title: Activity 1: Design show-and-tell (in class/async)
docs.text:
Before diving into technical skills, let's build design awareness by looking at real maps.

Steps:

  1. Share the inspirational map you brought—what makes it effective?
  2. As a group, identify design elements that work: color choices, hierarchy, labels, white space
  3. Discuss examples of maps that fail—what went wrong?
  4. Introduce design vocabulary: visual hierarchy, balance, contrast, accessibility

Build your inspiration library

Start collecting maps you admire (screenshots, bookmarks, Pinterest boards). Analyzing good design is one of the best ways to improve your own work.

docs.title: Activity 2: Style renewable energy data with classification methods
docs.text:
You'll join renewable energy data to countries and experiment with different classification methods to see how they change the story.

What is a CSV file?

CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is a simple spreadsheet format. It's just a text file where each line is a row and commas separate columns. You can open CSVs in Excel, Google Sheets, or any text editor.

Unlike shapefiles, CSVs don't have geometry (shapes)—they're just data tables. To map CSV data, you either:

  • Join it to a layer that already has geometry (like country boundaries)
  • Load it with coordinates if it has latitude/longitude columns

Steps:

  1. Download the renewable energy CSV (see pre-work checklist)
  2. Load it as a delimited text layer:
  3. Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Delimited Text Layer
  4. File name: browse to your CSV file
  5. Geometry definition: set to No geometry (attribute table only)
  6. Click Add, then Close

What does 'delimited' mean?

"Delimited" means the columns are separated by a character—usually commas (CSV) or tabs (TSV). QGIS detects this automatically.

  1. Join the CSV data to your countries layer:

What is a join?

A join connects two tables using a matching code. Think of it like a lookup:

  • Your CSV has data: AUS → 25% renewable
  • Your shapefile has shapes: AUS → [Australia polygon]
  • The join combines them: AUS → [Australia polygon] + 25% renewable

The code must match exactly. "AUS" won't match "Australia" or "aus".

  • Right-click countries layer → Properties → Joins tab
  • Click + to add a join
  • Join layer: your renewable energy CSV
  • Join field: the column in the CSV with country codes (e.g., "ISO_A3" or "code")
  • Target field: the matching column in Natural Earth (usually "ISO_A3")

  • Click OK

  • Verify the join worked:

  • Open the attribute table (right-click layer → Open Attribute Table)
  • Scroll right—you should see new columns from the CSV
  • If columns show NULL/blank, the codes didn't match (check spelling and capitalization)
  • Apply Graduated symbology:
  • Layer Properties → Symbology → Graduated
  • Value: renewable energy percentage field
  • Method: Try each one and observe the differences:
    • Quantile (equal number of countries per class)
    • Equal Interval (equal numeric ranges)
    • Natural Breaks (Jenks) (minimizes variance within classes)
  • Classes: 5
  • Color ramp: choose a ColorBrewer sequential palette (e.g., YlGnBu)
  • Compare the three methods—which tells the clearest story? Which is most appropriate for your data distribution?

No single right answer

Classification method choice depends on your data distribution and your message. Quantile ensures visual balance but can group very different values. Natural Breaks highlights genuine clusters but can create uneven class sizes.

docs.title: Activity 2.5: Classification as choice
docs.text:
Classification methods determine how your map groups data—and different methods tell different stories about the same numbers. This activity makes that visible.

The question to carry through this exercise: Who decided these groupings, and what does each choice emphasize?

Steps:

  1. With your renewable energy choropleth visible, note your current classification method and the class breaks shown in the legend
  2. Take screenshots of all three versions (you may already have them from Activity 2):

Version A: Quantile (Equal Count) - Classes: 5, Mode: Quantile - Note which countries fall into each class

Version B: Equal Interval - Classes: 5, Mode: Equal Interval - Note the legend values

Version C: Natural Breaks (Jenks) - Classes: 5, Mode: Natural Breaks - Note how breaks differ from the other methods

  1. Find a country with 15-20% renewable energy (like Germany or Japan) and check which class it falls into for each method. Does it appear "above average," "below average," or "middle"?

  2. Answer these questions:

  3. Which method makes differences between countries look largest?
  4. Which method makes a country with 15% renewable look best? Worst?
  5. If you were advocating for increased renewable investment, which method would support your argument?

The point isn't that maps lie

Maps don't lie—they answer specific questions. The skill is recognizing WHICH question each classification answers:

  • Quantile: "How does each country rank relative to others?"
  • Equal Interval: "How do countries compare to an absolute scale?"
  • Natural Breaks: "Where are the natural clusters in this data?"

Choose based on your question—and be explicit about your choice when presenting.

Reflection prompt: In your Week 2 reflection, describe how classification choice changed the story. Which method did you choose for your final map, and why?

docs.title: Activity 3: Add labels for major world cities
docs.text:
Labels turn abstract geography into recognizable places. You'll create smart labels that appear only when appropriate.

Steps:

  1. Add the world cities file:
  2. Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Delimited Text Layer
  3. File name: resources/data/processed/week02/worldcities.csv
  4. Geometry definition: Point coordinates → X field = lng, Y field = lat
  5. CRS: EPSG:4326 – WGS 84
  6. Click Add, then Close. The layer should appear in your Layers panel.
  7. Filter to major cities:
  8. Right-click layer → Filter...
  9. Expression: "population" > 5000000 (5 million+)
  10. Click OK
  11. Enable labels:
  12. Layer Properties → Labels tab
  13. Change No Labels to Single Labels
  14. Value: city name field
  15. Style the labels:
  16. Font: choose something readable (Arial, Open Sans, etc.)
  17. Size: 10-12 pt
  18. Buffer: Check "Draw text buffer" (white, 1-2mm) so labels stand out over the map
  19. Add scale-dependent visibility:
  20. In Labels tab, go to Rendering section
  21. Check "Scale dependent visibility"
  22. Maximum (most out): 1:50,000,000 (labels disappear when zoomed out beyond this)
  23. Minimum (most in): 1:100,000 (labels disappear when zoomed in too close)
  24. Zoom in and out to test—labels should appear at appropriate scales

Challenge: Use Expression-based labels to show both city name and population: - In the Labels tab, click the ε button next to Value - Enter expression: "name" || ' (' || format_number("population" / 1000000, 1) || 'M)' - This shows: "Tokyo (37.4M)"

docs.title: Activity 4: Scale city point sizes using population
docs.text:
Next, symbolise those same cities so marker size reflects population. The quick way in QGIS is to use Graduated symbology but switch the method to Size so the renderer handles all the math and legend work for you.

Steps:

  1. Duplicate the filtered cities layer from Activity 3 so labels stay untouched:
  2. Right-click the layer → Duplicate Layer → rename to Major Cities – Population Size.
  3. In the Layer Styling panel, use the drop-down menu at the top to switch the renderer from Single Symbol to Graduated (you can also open Layer Properties if you prefer the full dialog).
  4. Choose the population field for Value:
  5. Set Value to "population" / 1000000 so the classifier works in millions (the legend will read cleaner numbers like 5 M instead of 5,000,000)
  6. Set Mode: Quantile and Classes: 4
  7. Change the Method from Color to Size using the drop-down right under the class list. This tells QGIS to leave colour alone and only vary marker sizes.
  8. Click Classify so QGIS builds the ranges and previews the different symbol sizes.
  9. Finish the styling:
  10. Set Symbol size – Min = 2.5 mm, Max = 10 mm
  11. Choose one fill colour (e.g., coral) with a white 0.3 mm stroke so each class stays visually consistent
  12. Rename each class label to something friendly (e.g., 1–4 M, 4–8 M, 8–15 M, 15 M+). These labels feed directly into the legend.
  13. Match visibility with your labels:
  14. In the Rendering tab, tick Scale dependent visibility
  15. Use the same min/max scales as Activity 3 (e.g., 1:100,000,000 to 1:100,000)
  16. Click OK.
  17. Preview the legend: Layout ▶ Add Legend already pulls in the size classes. If you need more control, add Layout ▶ Add Item ▶ Data-defined size legend and select the Major Cities – Population Size layer so the legend lists sample sizes such as 5 M, 15 M, 30 M.

Need a gut-check?

Hover over cities with Identify Features to confirm a 30 M city draws noticeably bigger than a 5 M city. If not, either widen the min/max symbol sizes or reduce the number of classes so differences read clearly.

docs.title: Activity 5: Create a professional layout
docs.text:
Now you'll assemble everything into a polished, export-ready map.

Steps:

  1. Create a new Print Layout: Project ▶ New Print Layout... → name it "Renewable Energy Map"
  2. Set up your canvas:
  3. Right-click canvas → Page Properties
  4. Set to A3 Landscape (or your preferred size)
  5. Add the map:
  6. Add Map tool → draw a large rectangle covering most of the page
  7. Leave margins for title, legend, and credits
  8. Add a title:
  9. Add Label → draw a box at the top
  10. Text: "Global Renewable Energy Share by Country, 2023"
  11. Font: 20-24pt, bold
  12. Add a legend:
  13. Add Legend → draw a box (usually right side or bottom) for your choropleth and other layers
  14. In Item Properties, remove unnecessary items (uncheck layers you don't want shown)
  15. Rename legend items to be reader-friendly (not technical field names). The Major Cities – Population Size entry will already display the differently sized markers because the renderer is in Size mode; if you also added a dedicated data-defined size legend, position it directly beside the main legend for clarity.
  16. Add a scale bar:
  17. Add Scale Bar → draw at bottom of map
  18. Choose a style that matches your map aesthetic (single box, line ticks, etc.)
  19. Add an inset map (optional but impressive):
  20. Add Map → draw a small rectangle in the corner
  21. In Item Properties → Map 1, Lock layers and Lock styles
  22. Zoom this second map out to show global context
  23. Draw a rectangle shape showing the extent of your main map
  24. Add data credits:
  25. Add Label → small text at bottom
  26. Text: "Data: Natural Earth, Our World in Data | Map: [Your Name], 2024"
  27. Export:
  28. Layout ▶ Export as Image... → save to exports/week02_renewable_energy.png
  29. Layout ▶ Export as PDF... → save PDF version for print quality

Grid and guides

Use View ▶ Show Grid and View ▶ Show Guides to align elements precisely. Hold Shift while dragging to maintain proportions.

docs.title: Activity 6: Accessibility check
docs.text:
Make sure your map is readable by everyone, including those with color vision deficiencies.

Steps:

  1. Check color contrast:
  2. Visit a contrast checker (e.g., WebAIM Contrast Checker)
  3. Test your text colors against background colors
  4. Aim for WCAG AA standard (4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum)
  5. Simulate color blindness:
  6. Use a tool like Color Oracle or Coblis
  7. View your map through different color vision simulations
  8. Adjust your palette if categories become indistinguishable
  9. Check font sizes:
  10. Minimum 8-9pt for printed maps
  11. Minimum 10-12pt for screen display
  12. Write alt text (for future web publication):
  13. Draft a one-sentence description: "Choropleth map showing renewable energy share ranges from <5% (yellow) to >40% (dark blue), with highest adoption in Northern Europe and lowest in fossil fuel-producing nations."

docs.title: Graduated symbology shows no variation (all one color)
docs.text:
• Wrong field selected: Make sure you selected a numeric field, not text
  • All values are the same: Check the attribute table—does the column have variation?
  • Click Classify: You must click the "Classify" button after changing settings
  • Data type issue: If values imported as text, use Field Calculator to convert: to_real("field_name")

docs.title: Labels overlap or are unreadable
docs.text:
• Enable placement engine: Layer Properties ▶ Labels ▶ Rendering ▶ Check "Show all labels for this layer"
  • Use automated placement: Try Placement ▶ Mode ▶ Free (Angled) or Around Point
  • Add background: Labels ▶ Background ▶ Enable with white fill and small buffer
  • Scale-dependent visibility: Set labels to appear only at certain zoom levels in Rendering ▶ Scale-dependent visibility

docs.title: Color ramp doesn't look right
docs.text:
• Inverted colors: Click the dropdown arrow next to the color ramp → "Invert Color Ramp"
  • Wrong number of classes: Adjust the "Classes" number and re-classify
  • Custom colors needed: Click on individual class symbols to change colors manually

docs.title: Print Layout issues
docs.text:
• Map doesn't update: Click Refresh or check "Lock layers" is unchecked in Map Item Properties
  • Legend shows wrong items: In Legend Properties, uncheck "Auto update" and manually remove/rename entries
  • Scale bar is wrong: Check the map item's scale in properties, or set a specific scale
  • Export is blurry: Increase DPI to 300 for print quality in Export settings

docs.title: Can't find Layout Manager
docs.text:
• Open it: Project ▶ Layout Manager or Project ▶ New Print Layout
  • Layouts not saving: Layouts are saved within the .qgz project file—save your project

docs.title: CSV data won't join to shapefile
docs.text:
• Field type mismatch: Country names must match exactly (case-sensitive)
  • Encoding issues: Re-import CSV with UTF-8 encoding
  • Extra spaces: Use Field Calculator to trim: trim("field_name")

docs.title: Support materials
docs.text:
• Slides: Week 02 lecture deck
  • Template: Layout template guide
  • Toolbar reference: Quick styling tools
  • Dataset checklist: Week 2 items

docs.title: Reflect
docs.text:
Take 10-15 minutes to answer these questions in your Week 2 reflection:

  • Which classification method (quantile, equal interval, natural breaks) felt most appropriate for the renewable energy data? Why?
  • What design choices did you make in your layout (color, placement, hierarchy)? What impact do you think they have on the reader?
  • Did your map pass the accessibility checks? What adjustments did you make?
  • What was the most challenging part of creating the layout? What would you do differently next time?
  • Look at your Week 1 map versus your Week 2 map—what improved?

Attribution reminder

Always include data credits in your layout footer (e.g., "Data: Natural Earth, Our World in Data, SimpleMaps | Map: [Your Name], 2024"). Proper attribution is both ethical and often legally required.

docs.title: What you'll submit
docs.text:
• QGIS project file (projects/week02_symbology_layouts.qgz) with advanced symbology and labels configured
  • Exported layout: exports/week02_renewable_energy.png (or PDF) with all required elements
  • Your Week 2 reflection entry

Map submission requirements

Your exported map must include these four elements or it will not be accepted:

  • Title — What the map shows
  • Legend — What the colors/symbols mean
  • Scale bar — Distance reference
  • North arrow — Map orientation

See Map Design Principles for the complete checklist.

docs.title: Coming up next week
docs.text: Week 3 focuses on administrative and statistical boundaries, and you'll learn how to join socio-economic data (like SEIFA) to spatial layers. This is where GIS starts answering real-world questions about inequality, access, and demographics. Make sure you've downloaded your Week 3 datasets (SA2 boundaries and SEIFA, or local equivalents) so you're ready to hit the ground running.

docs.title: Research Question
docs.text:
"Which areas have the highest socioeconomic disadvantage, and how does this pattern change when we aggregate to different geographic scales?"

Boundaries shape how we understand social and economic patterns. The same data looks completely different when aggregated by suburb, municipality, or region. This week, you'll join socioeconomic index data to statistical boundaries and explore how geographic choices affect the stories we tell about disadvantage.

This is the same analysis you'll automate in Python during Week 8. By doing it manually first in QGIS, you'll understand exactly what each step accomplishes before writing code to replicate it.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you'll be able to:

  1. Identify which areas have the highest socioeconomic disadvantage by joining index data to boundaries.
  2. Perform attribute joins between polygon boundaries (e.g., SA2/LGA) and tabular datasets (e.g., SEIFA, ACS).
  3. Demonstrate how aggregating data to different geographic scales changes the patterns you see.
  4. Create derived indicators using the Field Calculator and critically interpret what they reveal—and hide.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Read: Understanding administrative boundaries—this provides essential context
  • Review the lecture: Boundary Systems & Data Joins
  • Think of one question about boundary changes or data comparability to discuss in class

Data downloads happen in class

We'll download SA2 boundaries and SEIFA data together as the first activity. Your facilitator will guide you through the process.

docs.title: Activity 0: One place, many maps
docs.text:
Before we start joining data, let's see how the same place looks completely different depending on what we map. This activity builds the critical lens you'll need for working with boundaries and socio-economic data.

The question: What stories can this place tell—and which ones become invisible with different data choices?

Steps:

  1. Choose a familiar area (your suburb, a place you've lived, or a well-known neighborhood)
  2. Load your SA2 layer and zoom to that area
  3. Create four different maps of the same place by styling different attributes:

Map A: Administrative identity - Categorize by state or LGA name - What official boundaries define this place?

Map B: Geographic hierarchy - Categorize by SA3 or SA4 region - Where does this place sit in the statistical hierarchy?

Map C: Population (if available) - Graduated symbology by population or area - Is this a dense urban area or sparse rural?

Map D: Your choice - After completing Activity 3 (join), return here and map by SEIFA decile - What socio-economic story does this place tell?

  1. For each map, note:
  2. What question does this map answer well?
  3. What does it hide or make invisible?

The point isn't that maps lie

Maps don't lie—they answer specific questions. The skill is recognizing WHICH question each map answers, and what other questions become harder to ask. You'll return to Map D after joining SEIFA data.

Reflection prompt: Each map shows the same geography but tells a different story. Which version feels most "true" to your experience of this place? Which could be misleading without context?

docs.title: Activity 1: Understand boundary hierarchies
docs.text:
Before joining data, you need to understand what your boundaries represent and how they relate to each other.

Steps:

  1. Load your SA2 (or equivalent statistical area) shapefile
  2. Open the attribute table and explore the fields:
  3. What's the unique identifier? (e.g., SA2_CODE_2021)
  4. What parent geographies exist? (e.g., SA3, SA4, state codes)
  5. What metadata is included? (area, population counts, names)
  6. Compare boundary types:
  7. Statistical boundaries (SA2, census tracts): designed for data collection and analysis
  8. Administrative boundaries (LGA, municipalities): used for governance and service delivery
  9. Postal areas (postcodes, ZIP codes): designed for mail delivery, not analysis
  10. Visualize the hierarchy:
  11. Color by a higher-level geography (e.g., SA3 or state)
  12. Notice how smaller areas nest within larger ones

Why boundaries matter

The boundary you choose affects your results. SA2 areas show local variation that disappears when aggregated to LGA level. Postcodes often cross meaningful boundaries and shouldn't be used for spatial analysis.

docs.title: Activity 2: Inspect and prepare your tabular data
docs.text:
You'll join SEIFA (or equivalent socio-economic index) data to your boundaries. First, make sure the data is clean.

Steps:

  1. Download your SEIFA (or ACS, deprivation index) CSV file
  2. Open it in a spreadsheet or text editor
  3. Check the structure:
  4. Does it have a geographic identifier that matches your shapefile? (e.g., SA2_CODE_2021)
  5. Are codes formatted consistently? (Watch for leading zeros: "00123" vs "123")
  6. What indicators are included? (IRSD, IRSAD, percentiles, etc.)
  7. Load into QGIS:
  8. Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Delimited Text Layer...
  9. Select your CSV file
  10. Geometry definition: "No geometry (attribute only table)"
  11. Click Add
  12. Open the attribute table and verify:
  13. Geographic codes appear as text (not numbers—leading zeros matter!)
  14. No unexpected missing values
  15. Field names are clear

Common pitfall: Leading zeros

Geographic codes like "01234" often lose their leading zero when opened in Excel, becoming "1234". This breaks joins. Always treat codes as text/strings, not numbers.

docs.title: Activity 3: Perform the attribute join
docs.text:
Now you'll link your socio-economic data to your spatial boundaries.

Steps:

  1. Right-click your SA2 layer → Properties → Joins tab
  2. Click the + button to add a new join
  3. Configure the join:
  4. Join layer: your SEIFA CSV layer
  5. Join field: the geographic code in the CSV (e.g., SA2_CODE_2021)
  6. Target field: the matching code in your shapefile (e.g., SA2_CODE21)
  7. Joined fields: leave blank to include all, or select specific indicators
  8. Custom field name prefix: optionally add "SEIFA_" to avoid field name collisions
  9. Click OK twice to close
  10. Open the attribute table of your SA2 layer—you should now see new columns from SEIFA
  11. Check a few rows to verify values look correct

Make the join permanent:

Joins are temporary by default. To save them: 1. Right-click your SA2 layer → Export → Save Features As... 2. Format: GeoPackage 3. File name: data/processed/week03/sa2_with_seifa.gpkg 4. Click OK

Why export?

Exporting makes your join permanent and faster to work with. The joined layer is now a single file you can share or reuse without worrying about the original CSV.

docs.title: Activity 4: Create derived indicators with Field Calculator
docs.text:
Raw index scores are useful, but you might want to create normalized rates, categories, or other calculations.

Steps:

  1. Open the attribute table of your exported layer (from Activity 3)
  2. Open the Field Calculator (calculator icon in toolbar or Ctrl+I)
  3. Example 1: Normalize by area
  4. Create output field: pop_density
  5. Output field type: Decimal (double)
  6. Expression: "population" / ("area_sqkm")
  7. Click OK
  8. Example 2: Categorize by decile
  9. Create output field: disadvantage_category
  10. Output field type: Text (string)
  11. Expression: 
    CASE
  WHEN "IRSD_decile" <= 2 THEN 'High disadvantage'
  WHEN "IRSD_decile" <= 5 THEN 'Moderate disadvantage'
  WHEN "IRSD_decile" <= 8 THEN 'Low disadvantage'
  ELSE 'Very low disadvantage'
END
  12. Click OK
  13. Example 3: Rate per 1,000 residents
  14. Create output field: rate_per_1000
  15. Expression: ("count_field" / "population") * 1000

Challenge: Create a field that flags areas in the bottom 20% for disadvantage AND top 20% for remoteness.

docs.title: Activity 5: Visualize and explore spatial patterns
docs.text:
Now that your data is joined, let's map it to see patterns.

Steps:

  1. Apply graduated symbology to your disadvantage index:
  2. Layer Properties → Symbology → Graduated
  3. Value: IRSD_score (or your disadvantage indicator)
  4. Method: Natural Breaks (Jenks)
  5. Classes: 5
  6. Color ramp: choose a diverging or sequential palette
  7. Click OK
  8. Explore the map:
  9. Where are the most disadvantaged areas?
  10. Do you see spatial clusters or random distribution?
  11. Are patterns related to urban/rural divides?
  12. Try different classification methods (Quantile, Equal Interval)—how does the story change?
  13. Use the Identify tool to click on specific areas and read their values

docs.title: Activity 6: Aggregate and summarize by geography
docs.text:
One of the most powerful GIS operations is aggregating data from one geographic level to another. You might count points per polygon, sum values when combining areas, or roll up detailed data to a larger region.

Key tools:

Tool What it does Example Count Points in Polygon Count features in each area Schools per LGA Join attributes by location (summary) Summarize any statistic spatially Sum population, mean income Dissolve Merge polygons + aggregate attributes Combine SA2s into SA3s with totals

docs.title: Part A: Count points in polygons
docs.text:
Steps:

  1. Load a point layer (e.g., schools, health facilities, or cities from Week 2)
  2. Run the count tool:
  3. Vector ▶ Analysis Tools ▶ Count Points in Polygon
  4. Polygons: your SA2 or LGA layer
  5. Points: your point layer (e.g., schools)
  6. Count field name: facility_count
  7. Output: save to data/processed/week03/sa2_facility_count.gpkg
  8. Open the attribute table—each polygon now has a count field
  9. Style by the count field using graduated symbology
  10. Interpret: Which areas have the most/fewest facilities? Does this relate to population or disadvantage?

docs.title: Part B: Summarize with spatial join
docs.text:
Steps:

  1. Open the Processing Toolbox (Processing ▶ Toolbox)
  2. Search for "Join attributes by location (summary)"
  3. Configure:
  4. Join to features in: your SA2 layer
  5. By comparing to: your point layer
  6. Geometric predicate: Intersects (or Contains)
  7. Fields to summarise: select relevant fields (e.g., capacity, size)
  8. Summaries to calculate: Count, Sum, Mean (select what makes sense)
  9. Output: save to data/processed/week03/sa2_with_summary.gpkg
  10. This is more flexible than Count Points—you can calculate multiple statistics at once

docs.title: Part C: Aggregate to roll up boundaries
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to roll up smaller areas into larger ones while calculating summary statistics. Let's start with a simple example using your Week 1 data, then apply it to boundaries.

Warm-up: Population by continent

Using your Natural Earth countries layer from Week 1:

  1. Open the Processing Toolbox (Processing ▶ Toolbox)
  2. Search for Aggregate (under Vector geometry)
  3. Configure:
  4. Input layer: ne_110m_admin_0_countries (your countries layer)
  5. Group by expression: "CONTINENT"
  6. Aggregates: Click ... to configure:
    • CONTINENT → First value
    • POP_EST → Sum
    • GDP_MD → Sum
    • NAME → Count (gives number of countries)
  7. Output: save to data/processed/week03/continents_aggregated.gpkg
  8. Click Run
  9. Open the result—you now have 7 polygons (one per continent) with:
  10. Total population per continent
  11. Total GDP per continent
  12. Count of countries per continent

What just happened?

You transformed ~177 country polygons into 7 continent polygons, with summarized statistics. This is the power of spatial aggregation—rolling up detailed data to answer bigger questions.

Now apply to boundaries: SA2 → SA3

The same technique works for statistical boundaries:

  1. Input layer: your SA2 layer (with joined SEIFA data)
  2. Group by expression: "SA3_CODE21" (or "LGA_CODE" for LGA-level)
  3. Aggregates:
  4. SA3_NAME21 → First value (keeps one name per group)
  5. population → Sum
  6. IRSD_score → Mean
  7. AREASQKM → Sum
  8. Output: save to data/processed/week03/sa3_aggregated.gpkg
  9. Compare the SA2 map to the SA3 map—what patterns become visible or invisible?

Aggregate vs Dissolve

Aggregate (Processing Toolbox) is better for calculating statistics—it has a clear interface for choosing sum, mean, count, etc. Dissolve (Vector menu) is simpler but hides the statistics options. Use Aggregate when you need to summarize numeric fields.

Aggregation changes the story

When you aggregate SA2 to SA3, you lose local variation. A disadvantaged pocket within an affluent SA3 becomes invisible. Always consider what level of detail your analysis question requires.

Challenge: Calculate a facility-to-population ratio:

  1. Use Field Calculator on your count output
  2. Expression: ("facility_count" / "population") * 10000
  3. This gives facilities per 10,000 people—a fairer comparison than raw counts

docs.title: Activity 7: Select and filter by attributes or location
docs.text:
You'll often want to focus on a subset of areas that meet certain criteria.

Steps:

  1. Select by attribute:
  2. Open attribute table → Select features using an expression (yellow button)
  3. Expression: "IRSD_decile" <= 2 (select most disadvantaged)
  4. Click Select Features
  5. Your map highlights selected areas in yellow
  6. Select by location:
  7. Vector ▶ Research Tools ▶ Select by Location...
  8. Select features from: SA2 layer
  9. That intersect: a custom boundary (e.g., Greater Sydney)
  10. Click Run
  11. Save selection:
  12. Right-click layer → Export → Save Selected Features As...
  13. Save to data/processed/week03/high_disadvantage_metro.gpkg
  14. Clear selection: Click Deselect All button or press Ctrl+Shift+A

Combining criteria

You can combine multiple criteria: "IRSD_decile" <= 2 AND "state" = 'NSW' selects only disadvantaged areas in NSW.

docs.title: Activity 8: Quality assurance and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Joins can fail silently. Always verify your results.

Steps:

  1. Check record counts:
  2. Original SA2 layer: _____ features
  3. SEIFA CSV: _____ rows
  4. After join: _____ features (should match SA2 count)
  5. Identify unmatched records:
  6. Open attribute table
  7. Sort by a SEIFA field (e.g., IRSD_score)
  8. Look for NULL values—these are SA2 areas that didn't match
  9. Common join issues:
  10. Mismatched codes: Check for leading zeros, extra spaces, different vintages
  11. Wrong field type: Ensure both join fields are text/string
  12. Different data years: 2021 boundaries don't match 2016 codes
  13. Document your work:
  14. Note which SA2 areas had no match (if any)
  15. Record assumptions (e.g., "Using 2021 boundaries with 2021 SEIFA")
  16. Save your notes in your Week 3 reflection

Boundary correspondence files

When boundaries change between census years, use correspondence files from ABS (Australia) or Census Bureau (US) to map old codes to new codes.

docs.title: Join shows 0 matched features
docs.text:
• Field names don't match: Check exact spelling, case, and spaces in both layers
  • Data types differ: One field is text, the other is number. Convert using Field Calculator: to_string("numeric_field") or to_int("text_field")
  • Leading zeros stripped: Excel often removes leading zeros from codes. Re-import CSV with the field formatted as text
  • Different vintages: 2016 census codes won't match 2021 boundary codes exactly

docs.title: Join shows partial matches (some NULL values)
docs.text:
• Spelling variations: "Sydney (City)" vs "City of Sydney" won't match
  • Extra spaces: Use trim("field_name") in Field Calculator to remove
  • Missing records: Some areas may genuinely have no data (e.g., unpopulated regions)
  • Check unmatched: After joining, filter for NULL values to see which records failed

docs.title: Joined fields disappear after saving
docs.text:
• Temporary join: By default, joins are stored in the project, not the layer. To make permanent:
  • Right-click the joined layer → Export → Save Features As...
  • Save as GeoPackage to data/processed/week03/
  • Add the new permanent layer to your project

docs.title: Field Calculator expression errors
docs.text:
• Syntax error: Check quotes—field names use double quotes "field", text values use single quotes 'value'
  • Division by zero: Wrap calculations in CASE WHEN "population" > 0 THEN ... ELSE 0 END
  • NULL values: Use coalesce("field", 0) to replace NULL with zero

docs.title: Choropleth map looks wrong after join
docs.text:
• Wrong field: Make sure you're mapping the joined field, not the original
  • NULL values showing: Set a default color for NULL/no data values in Symbology
  • Classification method: Try different methods (Quantile vs Natural Breaks) to see patterns

docs.title: Attribute table shows field names like "layer_field"
docs.text:
• Join prefix: QGIS adds the source layer name as a prefix. You can rename after exporting to a permanent layer
  • Too many fields: After joining, export only the fields you need to keep the table clean

docs.title: Your Research Findings
docs.text: After completing this week's analysis, summarize your findings:

docs.title: Research Question
docs.text: "Which areas have the highest socioeconomic disadvantage, and how does this pattern change when we aggregate to different geographic scales?"

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
Complete these based on your analysis:

  1. The SA2s with highest disadvantage (bottom decile) are: _________
  2. When aggregated to SA3 level, the most disadvantaged region is: _________
  3. I observed ______ (clustering / scattered distribution) of disadvantaged areas.
  4. The relationship between disadvantage and [urban/rural location, population density, or another variable] is: _________

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Data sources: ABS SA2 boundaries (ASGS 2021), SEIFA IRSD scores
  • Key parameters: Classification method: _, Number of classes: ___
  • Tools used: Attribute Join, Field Calculator, Aggregate/Dissolve

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
This analysis does NOT capture:

  • Change over time (single census snapshot only)
  • Variation within SA2 areas (could hide local pockets of disadvantage)
  • Why areas are disadvantaged (correlation vs causation)
  • How disadvantage relates to access to services

docs.title: QGIS ↔ Python comparison
docs.text: QGIS (Week 3) Python (Week 8) Layer Properties > Joins geopandas.merge() Field Calculator .assign() with expressions Dissolve / Aggregate tool .dissolve(by='column') Manual symbology geopandas.plot()

docs.title: If this were your capstone
docs.text:
• How would you adapt this for your study area?
  • What additional data would strengthen the analysis?
  • What research question would you ask?

docs.title: Support materials
docs.text:
• Slides: Week 03 lecture deck
  • Reading: Understanding administrative boundaries
  • Lecture notes: Boundary Systems & Data Joins
  • Python equivalent: Week 8 · Python Vector Workflows (automates this analysis)
  • Dataset checklist: Week 3 items
  • Reference: ABS correspondence files for boundary changes (link in lecture notes)

docs.title: Reflect
docs.text:
Take 10-15 minutes to answer these questions in your Week 3 reflection:

  • How do boundary choices affect the story your data tells? Compare what you see at SA2 vs LGA level.
  • When you dissolved SA2 to a larger geography, what patterns became visible? What local detail was lost?
  • What happens when boundaries change between census releases? How would you handle this in a longitudinal study?
  • Did your join work perfectly, or did you have unmatched records? What might explain the mismatches?
  • What spatial patterns did you observe in the socio-economic data? Were you surprised by anything?
  • Which boundary level (SA2, LGA, postcode, etc.) makes sense for your emerging capstone ideas? Why?

Document your troubleshooting

If you encountered join errors or data issues, write down what went wrong and how you solved it. These notes are incredibly valuable for future projects—and for helping classmates!

docs.title: What you'll submit
docs.text:
• QGIS project file (projects/week03_boundaries_joins.qgz) with completed joins
  • Joined boundary layer: data/processed/week03/sa2_with_seifa.gpkg (or equivalent)
  • Aggregated output: data/processed/week03/sa2_facility_count.gpkg or dissolved layer
  • At least one derived indicator created with Field Calculator
  • Exported map showing spatial patterns in socio-economic data
  • Your Week 3 reflection entry

Map submission requirements

Your exported map must include: Title, Legend, Scale bar, and North arrow. Maps missing any of these elements will not be accepted. See Map Design Principles.

docs.title: Coming up next week
docs.text:
Week 4 shifts from vectors to rasters with a flood risk assessment of the Hawkesbury-Nepean region. You'll work with digital elevation models (DEMs) to calculate slope, identify low-lying areas, and classify flood risk zones. This builds on your Week 3 boundary work—you'll use zonal statistics to summarize flood risk by SA2, combining terrain analysis with the administrative boundaries you now understand.

Week 4 ↔ Week 9 connection

In Week 4, you'll do the flood risk analysis manually in QGIS. In Week 9, you'll automate the same analysis in Python—the same parallel as Week 3 ↔ Week 8 for vector analysis.

docs.title: Research Question
docs.text:
"Which areas in the Hawkesbury-Nepean region are at elevated flood risk based on terrain characteristics?"

This week, you'll conduct a terrain-based flood risk assessment—the same analysis you'll automate in Python during Week 9. By doing it manually first in QGIS, you'll understand exactly what each step accomplishes before writing code to replicate it.

The Hawkesbury-Nepean region west of Sydney experienced devastating floods in 2022. While professional flood modelling uses complex hydrological simulations, terrain analysis provides a first approximation of flood-prone areas based on elevation and slope.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you'll be able to:

  1. Download and prepare elevation data (DEM) for a specific study area.
  2. Calculate terrain derivatives (slope, hillshade) that inform flood risk.
  3. Use the Raster Calculator to classify areas by flood risk level.
  4. Apply zonal statistics to summarize risk by administrative boundary.
  5. Communicate findings with appropriate limitations and caveats.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Review the lecture: Elevation & Surface Modelling
  • Read: Raster Data Basics

Data downloads happen in class

We'll download elevation data from ELVIS together as Activity 1. Your facilitator will guide you through the process—this is one of the more complex downloads in the course!

docs.title: Study area
docs.text:
We'll focus on the Hawkesbury-Nepean floodplain, approximately:

  • Bounding box: 150.6°E to 150.85°E, 33.65°S to 33.45°S
  • Why this area: Real flood history (2022 floods), varied terrain, recognizable to Sydney students
  • Size: Approximately 20km × 20km

For your capstone

You can adapt this workflow to any study area. The same approach works for bushfire risk (slope + aspect + vegetation), erosion risk, or accessibility analysis.

docs.title: Activity 1: Download DEM from ELVIS
docs.text:
You'll download elevation data from ELVIS (Elevation Information System), Australia's national elevation data portal.

Steps:

  1. Go to ELVIS
  2. Click Get Data or Order Data
  3. Navigate to the Hawkesbury-Nepean region (west of Sydney, around Richmond/Windsor)
  4. Draw a rectangle covering your study area:
  5. Keep it small (20km × 20km maximum) for faster processing
  6. Include the river floodplain and surrounding hills
  7. Select DEM as the product type
  8. Choose the highest resolution available (typically 5m for NSW)
  9. Download and save to week04/data/raw/
  10. Extract the ZIP file

What you should have:

week04/data/raw/
├── dem_tile.tif (or similar name)
└── (possibly metadata files)

Alternative: SRTM data

If ELVIS is unavailable, download SRTM 30m data from USGS EarthExplorer. It's lower resolution but covers the globe.

docs.title: Activity 2: Load and inspect the DEM
docs.text:
Before analysis, understand what your elevation data represents.

Steps:

  1. Load your DEM into QGIS: Layer ▶ Add Layer ▶ Add Raster Layer...
  2. Inspect layer properties:
  3. Right-click layer → Properties → Information tab
  4. Note the CRS (should be a projected CRS like EPSG:28356 for NSW)
  5. Check pixel size (resolution) and elevation range
  6. Style the DEM:
  7. Layer Properties → Symbology → Singleband pseudocolor
  8. Color ramp: terrain or Spectral (inverted)
  9. Click Classify then Apply
  10. Explore the terrain:
  11. Where is the river? (lowest elevations)
  12. Where are the hills? (highest elevations)
  13. Can you identify the floodplain? (flat, low-lying areas near the river)

Record these values:

  • Minimum elevation: _____ m
  • Maximum elevation: _____ m
  • Pixel size: _____ m

Check your CRS

If the DEM is in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326), reproject it first: Raster ▶ Projections ▶ Warp (Reproject) → Target CRS: EPSG:28356 (GDA2020 / MGA Zone 56)

docs.title: Activity 3: Generate a hillshade
docs.text:
Hillshade helps visualize terrain and will serve as a basemap for your final output.

Steps:

  1. Generate hillshade:
  2. Raster ▶ Analysis ▶ Hillshade
  3. Elevation layer: your DEM
  4. Azimuth: 315° (northwest—standard cartographic convention)
  5. Altitude: 45°
  6. Output: data/processed/week04/hillshade.tif
  7. Style the hillshade:
  8. Layer Properties → Symbology → Singleband gray
  9. This creates a shaded relief effect
  10. Layer it under your DEM:
  11. Move hillshade below the DEM in the Layers panel
  12. Set DEM transparency to 50-60%
  13. The combination shows elevation colors with 3D shading

QGIS ↔ Python comparison:

QGIS Python (Week 9) Raster > Analysis > Hillshade Custom function with np.gradient()

docs.title: Activity 4: Calculate slope
docs.text:
Slope tells us how steep the terrain is. Flat areas accumulate water; steep areas drain quickly.

Steps:

  1. Calculate slope:
  2. Raster ▶ Analysis ▶ Slope
  3. Elevation layer: your DEM
  4. Slope expressed as: Degrees
  5. Output: data/processed/week04/slope.tif
  6. Style the slope layer:
  7. Layer Properties → Symbology → Singleband pseudocolor
  8. Color ramp: YlOrRd (Yellow-Orange-Red)
  9. Min: 0°, Max: 30° (adjust based on your terrain)
  10. Click Classify then Apply
  11. Interpret the result:
  12. Yellow areas = flat (high flood accumulation risk)
  13. Red areas = steep (water runs off quickly)

Slope interpretation for flood risk:

Slope Risk implication <2° Very flat—water accumulates (HIGH RISK) 2-5° Gently sloping—some drainage 5-15° Moderate slopes—good drainage >15° Steep—rapid runoff (LOW RISK)

QGIS ↔ Python comparison:

QGIS Python (Week 9) Raster > Analysis > Slope np.gradient() + np.arctan()

docs.title: Activity 5: Identify low-lying areas
docs.text:
Low elevation is the primary flood risk factor. We'll create a binary raster showing areas below a threshold elevation.

Steps:

  1. Determine threshold:
  2. Look at your DEM's elevation range
  3. The floodplain is typically in the lowest 20-30% of elevations
  4. For the Hawkesbury, areas below ~20-30m are historically flood-prone
  5. Open Raster Calculator:
  6. Raster ▶ Raster Calculator...
  7. Enter expression to identify low areas: 
    "dem@1" < 30
  8. Replace dem with your actual layer name
  9. Replace 30 with your chosen threshold
  10. This creates a binary raster: 1 = low-lying, 0 = higher ground
  11. Save as data/processed/week04/low_lying.tif
  12. Style as categorized:
  13. 0 = transparent or light gray
  14. 1 = blue (flood-prone)

Choosing the threshold

The "right" threshold depends on local knowledge. For the Hawkesbury: - 1-in-100 year flood reaches ~15-20m in some areas - Major 2022 floods exceeded 20m at some gauges - Use 20-30m as a reasonable starting point

docs.title: Activity 6: Create flood risk classification
docs.text:
Now we combine elevation and slope into a composite risk score.

Flood risk logic: - Low elevation = higher risk (water accumulates) - Flat slope = higher risk (poor drainage)

Steps:

  1. Open Raster Calculator: Raster ▶ Raster Calculator...

  2. Step A: Normalize elevation to 0-1 (inverted so low = high score) 

    1 - ("dem@1" - [MIN]) / ([MAX] - [MIN])
    Replace [MIN] and [MAX] with your DEM's actual range.

Example for elevation range 0-200m: 

1 - ("dem@1" - 0) / (200 - 0)
Save as elevation_score.tif

  1. Step B: Normalize slope to 0-1 (inverted so flat = high score) 

    1 - ("slope@1" / 15)
    This gives score of 1.0 for flat (0°) and 0.0 for slopes ≥15° Save as slope_score.tif

  2. Step C: Combine with weights 

    0.6 * "elevation_score@1" + 0.4 * "slope_score@1"

  3. Elevation weighted 60% (most important factor)

  4. Slope weighted 40% Save as data/processed/week04/flood_risk_index.tif

  5. Step D: Classify into risk zones 

    ("flood_risk_index@1" < 0.3) * 1 +
("flood_risk_index@1" >= 0.3 AND "flood_risk_index@1" < 0.5) * 2 +
("flood_risk_index@1" >= 0.5 AND "flood_risk_index@1" < 0.7) * 3 +
("flood_risk_index@1" >= 0.7) * 4
    Save as data/processed/week04/flood_risk_classes.tif

  6. Style the classified output:

  7. Layer Properties → Symbology → Paletted/Unique values
  8. Assign colors:
    • 1 = Green (Low risk)
    • 2 = Yellow (Moderate risk)
    • 3 = Orange (High risk)
    • 4 = Red (Very high risk)

QGIS ↔ Python comparison:

QGIS Python (Week 9) Raster Calculator expressions NumPy array operations Multiple steps Single code block Manual classification np.where() conditions

docs.title: Activity 7: Zonal statistics by administrative boundary
docs.text:
To answer our research question, we need to summarize risk by area. "What percentage of each SA2 is at high flood risk?"

Steps:

  1. Load SA2 boundaries for your study area (from Week 3 or ABS download)
  2. Clip boundaries to study area if needed:
  3. Vector ▶ Geoprocessing Tools ▶ Clip
  4. Run zonal statistics:
  5. Processing ▶ Toolbox ▶ Zonal Statistics
  6. Raster layer: flood_risk_index.tif
  7. Vector layer: SA2 boundaries
  8. Statistics to calculate: Mean, Minimum, Maximum
  9. Output column prefix: risk_
  10. The SA2 layer now has new fields showing average risk per area

Calculate percentage at high risk:

  1. Create a binary "high risk" raster (classes 3 or 4): 

    "flood_risk_classes@1" >= 3
    Save as high_risk_binary.tif

  2. Run zonal statistics again:

  3. Raster layer: high_risk_binary.tif
  4. Statistics: Mean
  5. Prefix: pct_high_

The mean of a binary raster (0/1) equals the proportion of 1s. Multiply by 100 to get percentage.

  1. Style SA2 boundaries by pct_high_risk_mean:
  2. Layer Properties → Symbology → Graduated
  3. Color ramp: Reds
  4. This shows which SA2s have the highest proportion of high-risk land

docs.title: Activity 8: Create your flood risk map
docs.text:
Compile your analysis into a professional map layout.

Steps:

  1. Create a new Print Layout: Project ▶ New Print Layout... → name it "Flood Risk Assessment"
  2. Add your main map showing:
  3. Hillshade as the base (bottom layer)
  4. Flood risk classes (semi-transparent)
  5. SA2 boundaries (outlines only)
  6. Rivers/waterways if available
  7. Add a second map showing SA2s colored by % high risk
  8. Add map elements:
  9. Title: "Flood Risk Assessment: Hawkesbury-Nepean Region"
  10. Legend with clear risk categories
  11. Scale bar
  12. North arrow
  13. Data sources: "Elevation: ELVIS | Boundaries: ABS | Analysis: [Your Name], 2024"
  14. Methodology note: "Risk based on elevation (60%) and slope (40%). Does not include hydrological modelling."
  15. Export to exports/week04_flood_risk.pdf and .png

docs.text: After completing this analysis, summarize your findings:

  2. Approximately ____% of the study area is classified as high or very high risk.

docs.text:

  • Key parameters: Elevation threshold: m, Slope threshold: °
  • Weights: Elevation 60%, Slope 40%
  • Tools used: QGIS Raster Calculator, Zonal Statistics

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
This analysis does NOT capture:

  • Proximity to rivers and waterways
  • Drainage infrastructure and stormwater systems
  • Soil permeability and groundwater levels
  • Historical flood extent data
  • Hydrological flow modelling
  • Climate change projections

docs.title: If this were your capstone
docs.text:

  • What additional data would strengthen the analysis?

docs.title: DEM appears blank or all one color
docs.text:
• Stretch symbology: Right-click raster → Properties → Symbology → Set Min/Max to "Cumulative count cut" (2-98%)
  • NoData values: Large negative values (-9999) may skew the display

docs.title: Raster Calculator expression errors
docs.text:
• Check layer names: Use exact names as they appear in the Layers panel
  • Add @1: Every raster reference needs @1 suffix (e.g., "dem@1")
  • Parentheses: Ensure balanced parentheses in complex expressions

docs.title: Zonal statistics returns NULL
docs.text:
• CRS mismatch: Both layers must be in the same CRS
  • No overlap: Check that boundaries actually cover the raster extent

docs.title: Processing is very slow
docs.text:
• Clip first: Reduce raster extent before analysis
  • Lower resolution: Resample to 30m for testing, use full resolution for final output

docs.title: Support materials
docs.text:
